messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] DLM for Proportions/Multinomial Model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] DLM for Proportions/Multinomial Model
messages.body_plain:
Yes, the Dirichlet parameterization actually worked extremely well, at least for the initial application. When I tried applying the model to a problem where the proportions were very small, however, I started running into "vanishing density" problems, which I gather from previous posts is the consequence of getting too close to parameter constraints. I'm working on debugging them now, but I may re-post with more questions later.

Devin

On Thursday, January 30, 2014 10:17:34 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> Neat.  Did it work as expected?
>
> Both these models remind me of Blei and Lafferty's dynamic topic models, which are
> also time-series multinomials, although modeled quite differently:
>
>    http://www.cs.cmu.edu/~lafferty/pub/dtm.pdf
>
> Instead of modeling the evolution of the parameters for a Dirichlet-Multinomial,
> they use a logistic normal that evolves the actual multinomial
> parameter on the logit scale.  That's more like your first model.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> On 1/30/14, 4:30 AM, Devin Caughey wrote:
> > One more follow-up on this thread: Upon further reflection, I came to the conclusion that it would be more direct and
> > possibly more efficient to use a Dirichlet distribution for the dynamic component of this model. I therefore re-wrote
> > the model as follows:
> >
> > |
> > data {
> >      int<lower=1> T; // number of time periods
> >      int<lower=1> K; // number of categories
> >      int<lower=0> counts[T, K];
> > }
> > parameters {
> >      simplex[K] props[T]; // period-specific category proportions
> >      real<lower=1> priorN; // implied "sample size" of the previous period
> > }
> > model {
> >      for (t in 1:T) {
> >          if (t > 1) {
> >              props[t] ~ dirichlet(priorN * props[t - 1]); // transition equation
> >          }
> >          counts[t] ~ multinomial(props[t]);
> >      }
> > }
> > |
> >
> > Note that the parameter "priorN" plays roughly the same role as the innovation standard deviation parameter "tau" in the
> > earlier version of the model.
> >
> > ~Devin
> >
> >
> > On Friday, January 17, 2014 1:27:44 PM UTC-5, Devin Caughey wrote:
> >
> >     Code without the first line cut off:
> >
> >     |
> >     data {
> >          int<lower=1> T; // number of time periods
> >          int<lower=1> K; // number of categories
> >          int<lower=0> counts[T, K];
> >     }
> >     parameters {
> >          simplex[K] props[T]; // period-specific category proportions
> >          real<lower=0> tau; // innovation standard deviation
> >     }
> >     transformed parameters {
> >          vector[K] logit_props[T]; // logit of proportions
> >          for (t in 1:T) {
> >              for (k in 1:K) {
> >                  logit_props[t, k] <- logit(props[t, k]);
> >                  // Adjust for logit tranform by incrementing the log probability
> >                  // by the log of the derivative of the logit function
> >                  increment_log_prob(-(log(props[t, k]) + log1m(props[t, k])));
> >              }
> >          }
> >     }
> >     model {
> >          for (t in 1:T) {
> >              if (t > 1) {
> >                  logit_props[t] ~ normal(logit_props[t - 1], tau);
> >              }
> >              counts[t] ~ multinomial(props[t]);
> >          }
> >     }
> >
> >     |
> >
> >
> >     On Friday, January 17, 2014 1:25:22 PM UTC-5, Devin Caughey wrote:
> >
> >         Hi Bob,
> >
> >         Thanks for the correction. Your math is correct. The updated code is:
> >
> >         |
> >              int<lower=1> T; // number of time periods
> >              int<lower=1> K; // number of categories
> >              int<lower=0> counts[T, K];
> >         }
> >         parameters {
> >              simplex[K] props[T]; // period-specific category proportions
> >              real<lower=0> tau; // innovation standard deviation
> >         }
> >         transformed parameters {
> >              vector[K] logit_props[T]; // logit of proportions
> >              for (t in 1:T) {
> >                  for (k in 1:K) {
> >                      logit_props[t, k] <- logit(props[t, k]);
> >                      // Adjust for logit tranform by incrementing the log probability
> >                      // by the log of the derivative of the logit function
> >                      increment_log_prob(-(log(props[t, k]) + log1m(props[t, k])));
> >                  }
> >              }
> >         }
> >         model {
> >              for (t in 1:T) {
> >                  if (t > 1) {
> >                      logit_props[t] ~ normal(logit_props[t - 1], tau);
> >                  }
> >                  counts[t] ~ multinomial(props[t]);
> >              }
> >         }
> >         |
> >
> >
> >         Devin
> >
> >
> >         On Friday, January 17, 2014 9:02:46 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> >             I should've also added that the way to check all of this is
> >             to simulate data according to the model and make sure the
> >             Stan model can recover the parameters.
> >
> >             - Bob
> >
> >             On 1/17/14, 2:55 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >              > Sorry --- I just realized I gave you the Jacobian the wrong way around.
> >              > I'm used to going from unconstrained parameters to parameters,
> >              > which involves the inverse logit.  You're going the other way,
> >              > so you need to increment with the log absolute derivative of
> >              > the logits, not the inverse logits, that is:
> >              >
> >              >     log | d/dp logit(p) |
> >              >
> >              >      = log | d/dp log(p/(1-p)) |
> >              >
> >              >      = log | d/dp log(p) - d/dp log(1-p) |
> >              >
> >              >      = log | 1/p  + 1/(1-p) |
> >              >
> >              >      = log ( 1/(p * (1-p)) )
> >              >
> >              >      = - log (p * (1 - p))
> >              >
> >              >      = -[log(p) + log(1-p)]
> >              >
> >              >      = -[log(p) + log1m(p)]
> >              >
> >              > I'd check my work on that derivative, too.
> >              >
> >              > - Bob
> >              >
> >              > On 1/16/14, 8:59 PM, Devin Caughey wrote:
> >              >> Thanks Bob. Section 17 of the Stan manual is particularly helpful.
> >              >>
> >              >> Just to follow up, I rewrote my earlier model in two different ways. The first is similar to the first
> >             in that it
> >              >> entails a change of variables and thus requires a Jacobian adjustment:
> >              >>
> >              >> |
> >              >> data {
> >              >>      int<lower=1> T; // number of time periods
> >              >>      int<lower=1> K; // number of categories
> >              >>      int<lower=0> counts[T, K];
> >              >> }
> >              >> parameters {
> >              >>      simplex[K] props[T]; // period-specific category proportions
> >              >>      real<lower=0> tau; // innovation standard deviation
> >              >> }
> >              >> transformed parameters {
> >              >>      vector[K] logit_props[T]; // logit of proportions
> >              >>      for (t in 1:T) {
> >              >>          for (k in 1:K) {
> >              >>              logit_props[t, k] <- logit(props[t, k]);
> >              >>              // Adjust for logit tranform by incrementing the log probability
> >              >>              // by the log of the derivative of the inverse-logit
> >              >>              increment_log_prob(log(inv_logit(props[t, k])) +
> >              >>                                 log1m(inv_logit(props[t, k])));
> >              >>          }
> >              >>      }

> >              >>              logit_props[t] ~ normal(logit_props[t - 1], tau); //vectorized

> >              >>          counts[t] ~ multinomial(props[t]);
> >              >>      }
> >              >> }
> >              >> |
> >              >>

> >              >>      int<lower=1> K; // number of categories
> >              >>      int<lower=0> counts[T, K];
> >              >> }
> >              >> parameters {
> >              >>      vector[K] logit_props[T]; // logit of proportions
> >              >>      real<lower=0> tau; // innovation standard deviation
> >              >> }
> >              >> transformed parameters {
> >              >>      simplex[K] props[T]; // period-specific category proportions
> >              >>      for (t in 1:T) {
> >              >>          props[t] <- softmax(logit_props[t]);
> >              >>      }
> >              >> }
> >              >> model {

> >              >>      >> I'll leave the statistical modeling advice to others, but
> >              >>      >> I'd like to point out that your model isn't quite correct as formulated.
> >              >>      >> The problem is that you need to add the Jacobian of the inverse
> >              >>      >> logit transform to the total log probability.
> >              >>      >>
> >              >>      >> That'd be
> >              >>      >>
> >              >>      >>  for (k in 1:K) {
> >              >>      >>    logit(props[t, k]) ~ normal(logit(props[t - 1, k]), tau); // Gaussian on logit scale
> >              >>      >>    increment_log_prob(log(inv_logit(props[t,k])) + log1m(inv_logit(props[t,k])));
> >              >>      >>  }
> >              >>      >>
> >              >>      >> Here the Jacobian adjustment is the log of the derivative of the
> >              >>      >> inverse transform,
> >              >>      >>
> >              >>      >>  log | d/dp inv_logit(p) |
> >              >>      >>
> >              >>      >>    = log( inv_logit(p) * (1 - inv_logit(p) )
> >              >>      >>
> >              >>      >>    = log(inv_logit(p)) + log1m(inv_logit(p))
> >              >>      >>
> >              >>      >> where p = props[t,k].  We discuss the Jacobian for the logit in the
> >              >>      >> section of the manual on constraints and transforms (near the end).
> >              >>      >>
> >              >>      >> A more typical formulation I've seen is to parameterize props itself on the
> >              >>      >> logit scale (i.e., unconstrained vector[K] here), and then use softmax
> >              >>      >> to transform that to the parameter to plug into the multinomial.  Then you
> >              >>      >> don't need to fiddle with Jacobians.
> >              >>      >>
> >              >>      >> BUT, and this is a big but for now, our current softmax implementation has a memory
> >              >>      >> leak.  If your system's small, it probably won't matter.
> >              >>      >> We fixed it on the 2.1.1 hotfix branch on GitHub, but we haven't released the
> >              >>      >> code with the fix yet, as we had the same kind of memory leak in a few other
> >              >>      >> functions that we're going to fix.  In fact, I'm doing that in the other window
> >              >>      >> I have open now :-)
> >              >>      >>
> >              >>      >> You could also speed the model up a bit by vectorizing the call to normal, but I'd

> >              >>      >>
> >              >>      >> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 1/31/2014 3:33 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> HI, my quick hack would be to take the logit of the variable after transforming to a 0.5 to 4.5 scale, that is, work with logit((y - 0.5)/4).  This will make it continuous and will spread out the extremes a bit.  Of course it won't give correct predictions but otherwise it could do what you need.
> If it works (or if it doesn't), please let me know!
> A

I get this error:

  Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name,  :
    failed to parse Stan model 'stan_model' with error message:
  EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=14, column=21

     z <- logit((y-0.5)/4);
                      ^-- here

  DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
  no matches for function name="subtract"
      arg 0 type=real[1]
      arg 1 type=real
  available function signatures for subtract:
  0.  subtract(vector, vector) : vector
  1.  subtract(row vector, row vector) : row vector
  2.  subtract(matrix, matrix) : matrix
  3.  subtract(vector, real) : vector
  4.  subtract(row vector, real) : row vector
  5.  subtract(matrix, real) : matrix
  6.  subtract(real, vector) : vector
  7.  subtract(real, row vector) : row vector
  8.  subtract(real, matrix) : matrix
  expression is ill formed
  Parser expecting: <eps>

The relevant block is:
transformed data {
    real z[N];
    z <- logit((y-0.5)/4);
}

The error seems to indicate stan can't subtract a constant from a
vector, but that seems unlikely.

Ross

P.S. I've been running a truncated normal model, but it had poor n_eff
(3 for 200 iterations) in tests and is taking a long time in a
production run.

messages.subject: Re: Non-uniqueness of eigenvectors and implications for initializing model
messages.subject_clean: Non-uniqueness of eigenvectors and implications for initializing model
messages.body_plain:
On Friday, January 31, 2014 6:04:23 PM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
> I'm using an R script to generate reasonable initial values for the model variables. To get reasonable values for xi requires reproducing some of the computations used to produce that A matrix, including the computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of R*.
>
> There's the rub: I cannot reproduce in R the computation of the A matrix, because the eigendecomposition is not unique. Even if there are no repeated eigenvalues, and you normalize the eigenvectors, and you use a standard ordering of eigenvectors based on the eigenvalues, you can still multiply any subset of the eigenvectors by -1 and get another, equally valid, set of eigenvectors. There's no way I know of to guarantee that I'll get the same set of eigenvectors in R as I get in Stan.
>
> If anyone has any ideas for dealing with this problem, I would be very happy to hear them.

You could use RcppEigen and some C++ to do the eigendecomposition via Eigen from R.

Or you could flip things around so that the first row of the eigenvector matrix is strictly positive in both R and Stan.

Ben

 >   Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected becuase of the following issue:
 >   Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Scale parameter is 0:0, but must be > 0!
 >   If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the
 > sampler is fine,
 >   but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
 >

If you're talking about the "Informational Message" reports, those are NOT
errors, they are warnings.

Did you read the part that says

   "If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance
    matrices, then the sampler is fine,"

and if so, could you let us know how we can make it clearer that
this is just an informational message and not an error?

You're not the only one who's interpreted these messages as errors.
I think part of the confusion is that the embedded message says "error",
whereas we've tried to keep the referencing part clear that it's a warning.

But we want to keep them because if the rejections happen repeatedly,
then it can be a problem for sampling efficiency (up to the point where
if they happen in every step of every iteration the sampler won't move
at all).

I'm also wondering if users are familiar with the notion of Metropolis
rejection or if that's too much MCMC jargon.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the response!

We'd like to have lower=0 be exclusive, but floating point
just doesn't cooperate.  Instead, the exp(x) inverse transform
underflows to 0.

Then, when the value gets used as say, a scale for a normal
density, the density function throws an error.  That gets caught
further up the chain and turned into a Metropolis rejection and
the error message wrapped in that verbose and confusing message.

I suppose we could consider adding epsilon to the underflows and
doing the same for gradients, but that's much harder for constraints
like covariance matrices, where our big problems are with this
message and with inverse transforms.

- Bob

data {

messages.body_plain:
This is getting away from Stan so maybe it's not worth continuing this discussion on the models, but just briefly:
1. As Jennifer and I talk about in our book, it can be fine to fit a continuous model to discrete data, as long as the goal is not to predict individual values.
2. When you talk about multi modality, there are 2 things going on.  First, the data are discrete and lumpy so have lots of modes all over.  Second, there are lots of data near the beginning and end of the scale, so even a smoothed distribution of the data has 2 or 3 modes.  Tranforming to the logit scale will spread out the modes at the ends, indeed in some cases can spread out such modes so much that they are no longer modes.
A

I'm attaching the code and data. The R code with the problematic call

gp-fit-data.R. (This doesn't make a difference to the outcome.)

Also, a new clue: I've just gotten a new computer with a fresh install
of everything, and everything works fine. The same model fits with no
problem. I wonder if the problem was related to having installed R
with brew previously -- installing R with brew is a big mistake (lots
of things don't work), and I had quickly uninstalled it and installed
from the binary. But I may have left a bunch of the dependencies that
brew installed with it hanging around, which could have messed up some
compiler settings or something. Just a guess.

So: I still get the same errors on the old computer, but everything is
fine on the new one. Let me know if you'd like me to do anything on
the old one to help diagnose things. If that would be helpful, it'd be
easiest for me if we do it in the next week or so, as I'm likely to
give the old one to someone else at work.

real problem, although explaining it to other people might be a pain,
and it does make the console look ugly, so I can definitely see that
handling the situation another way could be nice if you think of a
good one.)

messages.body_plain:
> On Feb 1, 2014, at 10:48 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:

...

>> I don't see how the transform changes the fact the distribution is
>> discrete and multimodal.

Andrew answered this one.  Transforms affect modes.  It's
why maximum likelihood estimates are sensitive to parameterization.

>> Warning messages:
>> 1: In selectChildren(ac, 1) : error 'Interrupted system call' in select

...

>> I'm not really sure what to make of the interrupted system call
>> messages, which have not occurred in other, similar, calls.Presumably
>> they are coming from R's parallel library and the underlying OS, rather
>> than stan.  Perhaps they have something to do with this being a first
>> time experiment in which I ran more threads than physical cores (4),
>> though fewer than the virtual, hyperthreaded, cores.

No idea, but they're not coming from Stan.

>> At any rate, the computation did return 6 full sets of answers.  I'm a
>> little suprised n_eff isn't a bit better given the individual chains:

...

>> I'd expect n_eff to be more like the sum of the individual chain
>> n_eff's, or at least > than the largest single value.  Since chain 2 has
>> min n_eff of 31, how can all the chains together have smaller minimum
>> n_eff than chain 2 alone?

That's what you'd get with more tradition n_eff calculations,
but Stan's is more conservative, using both within-chain and
cross-chain measures.  You can see the definition in the Stan manual
and in the new edition of Gelman et al.'s Bayesian Data Analysis.

What you'll see is that higher R-hat will cause lower effective sample
sizes.  As R-hat goes to 1, the n_eff we calculate will converge to
calculating each chain independently and averaging.

- Bob

On 2/1/14, 7:31 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> On Sat, 2014-02-01 at 10:58 +0100, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> You get the error listed below because arithmetic is
>> not supported on arrays, only vectors.   Your y is
>> a one-dimensional array (real[1]) and 0.5 is real, and
>> real[1] - real is not allowed.  You can see the list of
>> signatures that are allowed in the warning message.
>>
>> Any suggestions on how to make that diagnostic message
>> clearer?  I think what would probably help is to back-translate
>> from the function name ("-" is replaced with the function "subtract").
>>
> I think the meaning of real[1] is less clear than the fact that
> "subtract"="-".  In this case the message could say "real array" or
> perhaps "real array[1]" or even "1-dimensional real array", but that
> might be too verbose for general use.

That's a good idea.  I don't want to be too verbose, but we can
do better than real[1].    I thought the
1 would be confusing.  Also, real[2] looks like an array of size
2, not a 2-dimensional array.

I created an issue to fix this in the future:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/529

> My problem was not that I didn't understand the message, but that I
> didn't believe it :)  That is, I thought combining arrays and scalars
> must be supported, and so either I had made an error, the system had
> made an error, or I had misunderstood the message.
>
> I think it would be nice if scalars and arrays could be combined.  I
> can't think of other examples where they can't (e.g., R, python numeric,
> C++ math libraries other  than stan, SAS IML).

Eigen's an example, and it's the C++ math lib we use :-)
You can wrap an array into a matrix or vice-versa, but you can't do
matrix arithmetic on arrays.

The reason we can't just automatically coerce back and forth is
that vectors are either row vectors (1 x K) or column vectors (K x 1),
so there's not an unambiguous way to cast an array without context.

We do allow them to mix in contexts like vectorized probability functions
where the use is unambiguous.

> Does this mean that, unless I have a good reason, I should prefer
> vector[n] x to real x[n]?

There's a chapter in the manual on when to prefer one over the other.
There's really no reason to have 1-dimensional real arrays other than
for generality of notation and similarity to BUGS.  There are substantive
differences between 2D arrays and matrices.  There are no integer
vectors or matrices, and only arrays can have 3+ dimensions.

- Bob

messages.subject: extracting parameters from optimization in RStan?
messages.subject_clean: extracting parameters from optimization in RStan?
messages.body_plain:
Calling the extract method on a stanfit object (returned by sampling or stan) puts the parameters in a very convenient form for working with. Is there a nice way to get the parameters resulting from optimizing in a similarly convenient form?

Naively, it seems to me like maybe it would make sense for the return value of optimizing to share a class with the return value of sampling. We do some of the same things with both types of fits, and I'd like the way I handle them to be similar. Maybe optimizing should give you a stanfit object with 1 chain and 1 iteration? Or maybe they're different subclasses of the same parent class?

I've pasted below an example session, and attached the code/data to run it (example is based on https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/tree/develop/src/models/misc/gaussian-process). At the bottom, you can see I faked a stanfit object by replacing the parameters from sampling 1 chain and 1 iteration with my optimized parameters. If I understand right, calling extract on that object did basically what I want. But obviously that's not ideal.

-David

I think structured output for optimizing() in RStan is
a very good idea, so I created a feature request:

   https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues/41

Users should feel free to submit feature requests, too.

CmdStan is set up so that the output of optimization and
MCMC are the same format, but those outputs are simple
CSV files with other material encoded as comments, and it's
not easy to extract structure from the headers.

If anyone wants to see this kind of thing happen (or other
things in RStan), we're always happy to take pull requests
(that come with reasonable test and doc) or welcome new dev
team members.  We're also happy to help out if you need
help getting started building features or understanding how
things are currently coded.

- Bob

I would like to point out this small Python package I wrote:

   https://github.com/JohannesBuchner/stagedstan

Unlike PyStan, it uses the make process of Stan (i.e. produces and runs executables), and actively stores outputs.

>From the Readme file:
StagedStan works similar to "make", namely in a deterministic fashion.
Runs consist of compilation, optimization and sampling (starting from the best fit).
When aborted, it continues where it was stopped.
Unlike PyStan, all results are stored in a file structure.
Each output is uniquely associated to the Stan code, data and seed used. If neither of them change, the result is not re-computed.
This also allows you to execute Stan on another machine, and to copy the output over.
StagedStan can parse the summary files of Stan runs, and write data dump files.
StagedStan allows the input of data from Python (e.g. numpy arrays).
Perhaps it is useful for someone else too. Fork and play around with it.

Kind regards,
         Johannes

Is there something non-deterministic about PyStan?

>   * Runs consist of /compilation/, /optimization/ and /sampling/ (starting from the best fit).
>   * When aborted, it continues where it was stopped.

This is tricky because we don't yet have a way in Stan to read in
the adaptation state and CmdStan only saves it in a comment in
the output CSV.  We're working on reading in the adaptation state so
it's possible to just generate more draws without having to rerun
adaptation.  (Having said that, the reason we didn't worry too much
about it the first time around is that if the initial effective sample
size or R-hat wasn't good enough, you usually want to rerun adaptation,
too.)

>   * Unlike PyStan, all results are stored in a file structure.

This should be possible in PyStan.  We're working on a consistent
set of functionality that we'll implement across (Py/R/Cmd)Stan.
It'll be a while before we get there, though.

>   * Each output is uniquely associated to the Stan code, data and seed used. If neither of them change, the result is
>     not re-computed.

Nice!

>   * This also allows you to execute Stan on another machine, and to copy the output over.
>   * StagedStan can parse the summary files of Stan runs, and write data dump files.
>   * StagedStan allows the input of data from Python (e.g. numpy arrays).

>
> Perhaps it is useful for someone else too. Fork and play around with it.

Thanks --- and feel free to post back here on updates.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Don't know if I sent this out --- it was stuck in
my drafts folder and I hadn't noticed.

Maybe someone else will know a simpler or more standard
way to achieve the same effect as

>    for (n in 1:N) {
>      y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
>      y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);
>    }

Looking more closely at your model, I think the real issue you're
having is that beta_x[n] and x are both parameters, which introduces
a serious non-identifiability issue.  You can multiply beta_x[n] by K and
multiply x by 1/K and you get the same answer.

The weak priors you have on the components aren't going to be enough
to pull them into line.  The fact that x has a hierarchical prior is
just going to push the problem up to mu_x and make it worse as far
as fitting goes.

Adding the second sampling distribution is going to pull x[k] back
toward the mean of the y[,k], providing a kind of identifiability.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi.  I’m trying to build a model with the Von Mises distribution in rstan, but so far it’s been crashed in <10 samples by a numeric overflow generated by boost::math::cyl_bessel_i<d>(d,d) (demo and session info attached).  I’m using a domain (-pi, pi) in the code, but the problem occurs with (0, 2pi) as well, and with a more restricted prior on kappa.

>From the list, it looks like the von_mises implementation is new in stan 2.0.x, so I’m guessing it hasn’t been used much and this is just due to a missing exception handler.  Could there be a different problem?

Thanks,

Nate

--

Nathanael Lichti

Postdoctoral Research Assistant

Forestry and Natural Resources

Purdue University

715 W. State St.

West Lafayette, IN 47907

nli...@purdue.edu

messages.body_plain:
I had seen that and posted a short reply (basically just agreeing with your evaluation of the issue). My reply seems to have disappeared, but I can still see your old reply. Kind of strange.

On Monday, February 3, 2014 10:36:19 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Don't know if I sent this out --- it was stuck in
> my drafts folder and I hadn't noticed.
>
> Maybe someone else will know a simpler or more standard
> way to achieve the same effect as
>
> >    for (n in 1:N) {
> >      y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
> >      y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);
> >    }
>
> Looking more closely at your model, I think the real issue you're
> having is that beta_x[n] and x are both parameters, which introduces
> a serious non-identifiability issue.  You can multiply beta_x[n] by K and
> multiply x by 1/K and you get the same answer.
>
> The weak priors you have on the components aren't going to be enough
> to pull them into line.  The fact that x has a hierarchical prior is
> just going to push the problem up to mu_x and make it worse as far
> as fitting goes.
>
> Adding the second sampling distribution is going to pull x[k] back
> toward the mean of the y[,k], providing a kind of identifiability.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
> On 1/27/14, 8:49 PM, John Hall wrote:
> > Bob,
> > I can't say that if I wrote down what I thought I was trying to do (at least a simple version of what I'm trying to do),
> > I would have that written down, but that's probably because I am self-taught on Bayesian statistics (my MA degree did
> > not cover the subject one iota). Nevertheless, it's the first thing I've done that's giving me the correct results using
> > one Stan file, which makes it feel right.
> >
> > If you recall above, I had wanted to cross-sectionally estimate some means in each period in one Stan file and then pass
> > the distribution of those means to another Stan fit statement. This approach seems to ensure that this takes place since
> > it constrains the x's with respect to the y's. For instance, had I just fit
> > p(y[n,k] | x, std_y, mu_y, beta_x[n], x[k])=normal(y[n,k] | mu_y + beta_x[n] * x[k], std_y)
> > then there are too many parameters in mu_y + beta_x[n] * x[k]. If there's a better way to get the same results without
> > this approach, I'm all ears.
> >
> > On Monday, January 27, 2014 1:59:54 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> >
> >
> >     On 1/27/14, 5:41 PM, John Hall wrote:
> >      > I think I've stumbled across what I needed, albeit it's a little slow. A simple set of code is below (using just one
> >      > index). This approach can be used for hierarchical models when you want to be able to model some kind of systematic
> >      > factor and exposures to such a factor. My example was meant for an asset pricing model (in finance) that estimates a
> >      > bottom-up market factor instead of using the observed market returns.
> >      >
> >      > I generated some x's that are effectively the cross-sectional mean in each period of the y's. I then regress each
> >     of the
> >      > y's against x. Importantly, I do this in two separate steps to ensure the x's will be tied down.
> >      >
> >      > When I was originally trying to get this to work in one Stan file, I had tried this format, but crucially without
> >     the
> >      > first y statement (which I can seem to only be able to do in the loop).
> >
> >     Yes, we only vectorize one-dimensional arrays.  We're going
> >     to add higher dimensional ones in the future, with the same
> >     requirements on matching shapes as we have now.
> >
> >      > This led to there being too many parameters.
> >      > While the x's in that method may have been correlated with the original data used to generate the data, they had
> >      > significantly different means (perhaps even different signs) and variances. This led to the beta_x's and mu_y's
> >     being
> >      > way off what is sensible, even if they would produce the correct posterior predictive distributions. Including
> >     the first
> >      > y statement ties everything down.
> >
> >
> >
> >       >    for (n in 1:N) {
> >       >      y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
> >       >      y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);
> >       >    }
> >
> >
> >     What this is doing is saying that
> >
> >          p(y[n,k] | x, std_y, mu_y, beta_x[n], x[k])
> >
> >            = normal(y[n,k] | x[k], std_y) * normal(y[n,k] | mu_y + beta_x[n] * x[k], std_y)
> >
> >     Is that really what you wanted to do?
> >
> >     - Bob
> >
> >      >
> >      > data {
> >      >    int<lower=0> N;
> >      >    int<lower=0> T;
> >      >    vector[T] y[N];
> >      > }
> >      >
> >      > parameters {
> >      >    real mu_x;
> >      >    real<lower=0> var_x;
> >      >    vector[T] x;
> >      >    real beta_x[N];
> >      >    real mu_y;
> >      >    real<lower=0> var_y;
> >      > }
> >      > transformed parameters {
> >      >    real<lower=0> std_x;
> >      >    real<lower=0> std_y;
> >      >
> >      >    std_x <- sqrt(var_x);
> >      >    std_y <- sqrt(var_y);
> >      > }
> >      > model {
> >      >    mu_x ~ normal(0, 100);
> >      >    var_x ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
> >      >    x ~ normal(mu_x, std_x);
> >      >    beta_x ~ normal(0, 100);
> >      >    var_y ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
> >      >    mu_y ~ normal(0, 100);
> >      >
> >      >    for (n in 1:N) {
> >      >      y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
> >      >      y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);
> >      >    }
> >      > }
> >      >
> >      >
> >      > On Tuesday, January 14, 2014 5:07:02 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >      >
> >      >     On 1/14/14, 3:02 AM, John Hall wrote:
> >      >      > For the Gibbs thing, I was just summarizing how I write the program to do the Gibbs sampling more than
> >     anything. I
> >      >      > typically would write seperate functions for estimating the distribution for a parameter and simulating
> >     from that
> >      >      > distribution. It's the same thing as what you're talking about though, just as separate steps.
> >      >
> >      >     You can do that in Stan using the generated quantities block.
> >      >     The parameters are declared as parameters, the model is in
> >      >     the model, then the quantities to generate conditional on
> >      >     the parameters are declared and defined in the generated quantities
> >      >     block.
> >      >
> >      >     This is one of the reasons we built the generated quantities --- to
> >      >     generate predictive quantities based on the parameters.
> >      >
> >      >     If you do Gibbs, you have to have the joint probability anyway,
> >      >     assuming your model's consistent --- the conditionals should
> >      >     be conditionals of a joint probability.  Technically, all you
> >      >     need is something proportional to the posterior p(parameters|data),
> >      >     which itself is proportional to the joint p(parameters,alpha) by
> >      >     Bayes's rule.  Sorry if this is all obvious.
> >      >
> >      >     - Bob
> >      >
> >      >      > On Monday, January 13, 2014 7:15:01 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >      >      >
> >      >      >     Yes, Stan requires you to write down the full probability
> >      >      >     function as does any kind of full Bayesian modeling.
> >      >      >
> >      >      >     Your algorithm sketch doesn't look like a Gibbs sampler to me.
> >      >      >     If you have N parameters theta[1],...,theta[N], and full probability
> >      >      >     function p(theta[1],...,theta[N]),  then Gibbs initializes theta, then
> >      >      >     does
> >      >      >
> >      >      >     for (i in 1:I)
> >      >      >         for (n in 1:N)
> >      >      >           sample theta[n] from p(theta[n] | theta[1],..,theta[n-1],theta[n+1],...,theta[N])
> >      >      >
> >      >      >     I don't understand your estimate/simulate notation.
> >      >      >
> >      >      >     The short answer is that you can't mix simulation and sampling
> >      >      >     in Stan.  You can sample and do simulations based on the samples,
> >      >      >     but you can't then feed the simulations back into the sampler in any way.
> >      >      >
> >      >      >     - Bob
> >      >      >
> >      >      >
> >      >      >
> >      >      >
> >      >      >
> >      >      >     On 1/14/14, 12:39 AM, John Hall wrote:
> >      >      >      > Thanks for the reply Bob. I hadn't used BUGS before using Stan and had just coded my own Gibbs
> >     samplers, so I
> >      >      >     thought
> >      >      >      > this would be easier to attach what I've been working on (I have it set up so the un-rar'ed folder
> >     is in
> >      >     C). I also
> >      >      >      > sketched a Gibbs sampler of what I'm trying to do below, more or less. The S_test_stan.r file is
> >     the main
> >      >     file.
> >      >      >     It calls
> >      >      >      > the S_gen_data.r file to create the data and then fits some Stan models.
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      > The key line is 60:
> >      >      >      > y_sim_index_cutdown <- colMeans(aperm(y_sim_index, c(2, 1, 3)))
> >      >      >      > In the previous section, I fit the Stan model cross-sectionally as I described above. The y_sim_index
> >      >     variable is
> >      >      >     the
> >      >      >      > array containing all these results. Thus, this line is like taking the posterior mean in each period
> >      >     (which is
> >      >      >     what you
> >      >      >      > seem to recommend). I then use these means in subsequent analysis, treating them as though they are
> >      >     observed data.
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      > In a Gibbs sampler, I could just use the y_sim_index posterior samples directly in the next stage
> >     of the
> >      >      >     analysis. For
> >      >      >      > instance, the following sequence I give a headline of "Fit Simple Hierarchical Model with Index as
> >      >     Regressor" in the
> >      >      >      > code regresses the y_bottom variable against the respective index (calculated by that line 60
> >     above). In a
> >      >     Gibbs
> >      >      >      > sampler, in an iteration I can use the y_sim_index in the next line (see sketch). It seems like the
> >      >     impression I'm
> >      >      >      > getting is that Stan requires the formula for the distribution. I'm wondering if that's the case or if
> >      >     there's
> >      >      >     any way
> >      >      >      > to use simulated variables at all the way I would with Gibbs sampling.
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      > I'm essentially throwing away all the rest of the information about the uncertainty in these means. I
> >      >     considered
> >      >      >     that I
> >      >      >      > could calculate the covariance in each time period and assume that the measurement error is
> >     multivariate
> >      >     normal. I'm
> >      >      >      > worried that this might be slow (I can't even get the multivariate normal-inverse Wishart
> >     distribution to
> >      >     work
> >      >      >      > properly), but it seems possible. For this type of data, multivariate normal seems like a good
> >     assumption,
> >      >     but it
> >      >      >     may
> >      >      >      > not always make sense.
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      > Gibbs sketch:
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      > for i in 1:(n_burn+n_gibbs) {
> >      >      >      >    #cross-sectional estimation
> >      >      >      >    for j in 1:n_j {
> >      >      >      >      for t in 1:T {
> >      >      >      >        estimate x[t, j], the mean in each time period t for group j of variable y
> >      >      >      >        simulate x[t, j]
> >      >      >      >      }
> >      >      >      >    }
> >      >      >      >    # time-series estimation
> >      >      >      >    for n in 1:N {
> >      >      >      >      for equation: y[n] ~ N(beta_y[n] * x[index[n]], sigma[n]^0.5)
> >      >      >      >      estimate beta_y[n]
> >      >      >      >      simulate beta_y[n]
> >      >      >      >      estimate sigma[n]
> >      >      >      >      simulate sigma[n]
> >      >      >      >      Note the x's are all from the cross-sectional step above. They change with each Gibbs iteration.
> >      >      >      >    }
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      >    if i>n_burn {
> >      >      >      >      save relevant variables
> >      >      >      >    }
> >      >      >      > }
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      > On Saturday, January 11, 2014 3:28:17 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      >     I'm also a little unclear on what the problem is.
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      >     Are you asking whether we can do cut like in BUGS?
> >      >      >      >     The closest we can come is using the generated quantities
> >      >      >      >     block to generate new variables based on fitted values.
> >      >      >      >     It uses the parameters in each sample, so propagates that
> >      >      >      >     uncertainty.
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      >     For example,
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      >         data {
> >      >      >      >           int N;
> >      >      >      >           real y[N];
> >      >      >      >           int N_sim;
> >      >      >      >         }
> >      >      >      >         parameters {
> >      >      >      >           real mu;
> >      >      >      >           real<lower=0> sigma;
> >      >      >      >         model {
> >      >      >      >           y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
> >      >      >      >         }
> >      >      >      >         generated quantities {
> >      >      >      >           real y_sim[N_sim];
> >      >      >      >           for (n in 1:N_sim)
> >      >      >      >             y_sim[n] ~ normal_rng(mu,sigma);
> >      >      >      >         }
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      >     This fits the parameters mu and sigma based on the data
> >      >      >      >     y, then generates M new variates y_sim.  There's no feedback
> >      >      >      >     from the generated quantities to the model.  If you instead
> >      >      >      >     declared y_sim as a parameter and included
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      >          y_sim ~ normal(mu,sigma);
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      >     in the model, then you do joint inference for (mu,sigma,y_sim).
> >      >      >      >     In this case, I think the answers should be equivalent other than
> >      >      >      >     that generated_quantities will be more efficient --- it shouldn't change
> >      >      >      >     your inferences for mu and sigma.

messages.body_plain:
You're right --- I don't think it's gotten a lot of play (or obviously
enough testing).

Do you know what values of y, mu and kappa are causing the problem?
You could replace

  y ~ von_mises(mu, kappa);

with

  print("mu=",mu);
  print("kappa=",kappa);
  for (n in 1:N) {
     print("n=",n, "; y=",y);
     y[n] ~ von_mises(mu, kappa);
  }

We should at least be catching that exception and just rejecting
the sample as of the next release (2.2.0).  We weren't previously catching
all the errors thrown by Boost functions.

We were hoping to get 2.2.0 out this week, but our continuous integration
server is being flaky and we're all swamped with side projects.  (Excuses,
excuses, I know.)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Explaining a bad chain (teaching example)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Explaining a bad chain (teaching example)
messages.body_plain:
You don't even need to bother with sampling to see what's
going wrong.  Just look at the probabilty mass in the posterior,
which is proportional to the log probability function by Bayes's
rule.  I believe in this case, you can calculate the posterior
analytically.

The general problem with the improper prior on sigma and mu
is that most (as in infinitely much of) of the probability mass
is away from the values you want, namely in a neighborhood
around mu = 0, sigma=1.

To get a feeling for what's going on geometrically in Stan, you need
to look at the probability function on the unconstrained space,
which log-transforms sigma (and performs the appropriate Jacobian
adjustment).

Then think of the log probability function on the unconstrained space
as a bowl and the parameter vector as a marble.
Now consider what happens when you thwack the marble in a random
direction and let it go for a fixed amount of time.  That's essentially
what HMC is doing.  You don't have to worry about NUTS to see the problem.

You might want to contrast the geometry with what you get by duplicating
the data points, starting with (1,1,-1,-1) and continuing.  You'll see
the geometry begin to look reasonable around the neighborhood where you
want the estimate to be.

- Bob

I appreciate the enthusiasm, Andrew.  Thanks!

Bob, I inserted the print statements and ran some more tests.  It looks like the issue is with large values for kappa. I tried inserted

  print("besselI = ", modified_bessel_first_kind(0, kappa));

in the model statement before the sampling loop that you suggested, and that also caused the error.  So I changed the model to

data{
  int<lower = 0> N;
  real<lower = 0> kappa;
}
parameters{
  real mu;
}
model{

  for (n in 1:N) {

     print("n=",n, "; y=", kappa[n]);
     print("besselI = ", modified_bessel_first_kind(0, kappa[n]));
     increment_log_prob(normal_log(kappa[n],mu , 1));

And used data,

This produced the error at n = 9, kappa = 1096.63.  The preceding value (kappa = 403.429) gave Bessel I = 3.19e+173.

Do the boost functions have the option to work on an exponential scale?  If so, that could solve the issue.  For example, see the BesselI function in the R package Bessel.

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for your comments, Bob.

When referring to continuation, I did not mean it as fine-grained as you describe.

As you point out, the goals can be achieved with PyStan as well. However, I found the need to control individual stages in more detail (e.g. compile flags, and debugging intermediate products).
Additionally, I had trouble avoiding recompilation and running from initial parameters -- although the API promises that this should be possible. I can't say I have a detailed bug report though.

I was rather confused that the best-fit parameter file that is written by "optimize" can not be used as a init file.
For my problem, the sampling phase hangs for me often for a long time at "Iteration:    1 / 1000 [  0%]  (Warmup)", where I believe it tries to optimize to a good starting point.
So I would like to first optimize, visualize that point, and continue sampling from there, then visualizing the uncertainties.
In StagedStan I implemented reading Stan output files and writing R dump data files, so this is solved this way. Perhaps there is a smarter way I don't know about.

One possible benefit of going through executables (rather than compiling in memory) is that those can be deployed to multiple machines, and the optimized output files can be computed there. That's not so easy to do directly in Python, but with the staged approach, the Python program can pick up the results and continue.
I'm not saying that this can't be achieved by PyStan, but rather that there are two ways of doing it, and they can exist separately.

Speaking of PyStan, accessing the likelihood function would be nice, i.e. evaluating the likelihood + gradient from Python.

Thank you for taking the time.

Cheers,
             Johannes

> set of functionality that we'll implement across (Py/R/Cmd)Stan.
> It'll be a while before we get there, though.
>
> >   * Each output is uniquely associated to the Stan code, data and seed used. If neither of them change, the result is
> >     not re-computed.
>
> Nice!

>

see:  http://www.boost.org/users/history/version_1_55_0.html

I don't see anything that would let it work on the log scale.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Linas,

To my understanding, this is not really an error but a more of a message. Apparently, the sampler got someplace very close to the bounds of the sampling space and tried stepping outside, resulting in a value that lgamma could not evaluate. This should not be bad if it only happens a few times. I haven't looked at the attachment, but make sure that the support for all your parameters is well defined and in line with the bounds on your priors (if there are any). You should only worry if you repeatedly get messages like this; this could (or always does?) indicate that the parameter support is ill-defined (ie the bounds on your parameters in the parameters block).

Luc

messages.body_plain:
Sorry - that should have been defined as kappa[N].  Typo in the email.

A kappa of 400 corresponds to a standard deviation of about 3 degrees or 0.05 radians.  So depending on the application, much higher values might be reasonable.  In my case, I'm modeling error in directional measurements for mapping data, and it's plausible that in some cases most errors may be as small as 0.1 degree, which would give a kappa > 1e7.  Happily, I'm also working with short distances, so there's not any practical difference between a 3 degree error and an 0.1 degree error once I translate back to an (x,y) plane.  If I need to, I can just put an upper limit on kappa to prevent the overflow, but it would be nice to have an unbiased estimate of precision.

I'll try updating boost and see if that works, and if not, I'm going to try  rescaling the measurements with a redundant parameterization.  Will let you know how it goes in a few days.  Thanks for the help.

messages.body_plain:
Every time you add a distribution to your model you introduce a bit of overhead, both in actually computing the density and its gradient with our autodiff code.  For large models (tens of thousands of observations counts as reasonably big) this overhead is significant.

When you vectorize, however, that overhead is drastically slashed.  For example, we can share intermediate evaluations and avoid redundant calculation.  The biggest gain is from the autodiff overhead -- and given the number of observations you have a few orders of magnitude improvement is not surprising.

So, yes, having lots of deterministic temporaries in memory to admit vectorization is worth it given the way Stan works under the hood.

On 2/5/14, 2:04 PM, Tamas Papp wrote:
> Hi,
>
> How can I query the Rhat for a stanfit object in rstan? The print method
> displays it, but I would like to access it for a plot. I looked at the
> code but got lost, it seems to be saving it somewhere in a cache.

If fit is the stanfit object, you can use summary(fit)$summary
to pull out the summary statistics.

For example,

 > labels(summary(fit)$summary)
[[1]]
[1] "y"    "lp__"

[[2]]
  [1] "mean"    "se_mean" "sd"      "2.5%"    "25%"     "50%"     "75%"     "97.5%"   "n_eff"   "Rhat"

First arg is variable and second arg is summary stats.

And then

 > summary(fit)$summary[1,10]
[1] 1.001408

gives you the Rhat for y.  I'm sure there's a more elegant way to do this
in R.

> By the way, maybe it could print more digits by default? Rhat=1 is
> reassuring, but I am always wondering whether that is 1.4 or 1.004,
> rounded to 1. I found that
>
> print(fit, digits=4)
>
> prints the whole thing, but maybe two digits after the decimal dot by
> default would be informative.
>

Thanks for the reminder.  We've been meaning to do that.  I created
an issue:

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues/44

We want to go with digits=3 in order to test Rhat < 1.05, which is
Andrew's default recommendation.  He likes fewer digits, but we've
compromised on 3.

- Bob

Hi, Juan.  I'm ccing the Stan users and Stan developers lists because these are important general questions.  Here are my answers:

1.  For examples of multilevel modeling (which can be viewed as Bayesian) see my book with Hill.
For many more examples of Bayes, see by book with Carlin et al.
For management in particular, you could see this forthcoming article:  http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/bayes_management.pdf

2.  There's Bayesian Data Analysis and the Stan manual.  Beyond that, no tutorial materials.  Bob and I are talking about writing a Statistics Using Stan book but this hasn't happened yet.  We do have plans for Stan short courses, though.  We will charge money for these; they are a way for us to raise funds to support the Stan project.

A

messages.subject: RE: [stan-users] numeric overflow in Von Mises distribution
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] numeric overflow in Von Mises distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hi.  I haven't tested boost 1.55 yet, but I found a couple of workarounds that do the job with 1.54.  The first was to rescale the data to an interval of 2*pi, fit the von Mises, and estimate kappa from a back-transformed posterior predictive sample (code below).  However, because Stan includes conditional processing (I love this!), a cleaner solution uses the fact that asymptotically, as  kappa -> Inf, VM(mu, kappa) -> N(mu, sqrt(1/kappa)).  So this code yields very good results as long as kappa_star is reasonable:

data{
  ... define N, y ...
  real<lower = 0> kappa_star;    // e.g., 100; use normal approx. for kappa >= kappa_star
}
...
model{
  for(n in 1:N){
    if(kappa < kappa_star)
      increment_log_prob(von_mises_log(y[n], mu, kappa));
    else
      increment_log_prob(normal_log(y[n], mu, sqrt(1/kappa)));    // normal approximation
  }
}

By the way, I tried using vectorized sampling statements in place of the manual increment, and with kappa = 2e6, Stan slowed to the point that I thought it had hung.  I only tried it once, so it could have just been a coincidence.  With kappa = 2, the vectorized version was about 5 seconds faster over 1000 draws.

- Nate

Here's code for the first approach:

data{
...
int<lower = 0> M;                               // number of posterior predictive samples generate
}
...
transformed data{
  real<lower = 0, upper = 2 * pi()> z[N];
  real<lower = 1> scale_factor;

  scale_factor <- 2 * pi() / (max(y) - min(y));
  for(n in 1:N)
    z[n] <- (y[n] - min(y)) * scale_factor;
}
... define mu_z and kappa_z parameters ...
model{
  z ~ von_mises(mu_z, kappa_z);
}
generated quantities{                                                    // assuming syntax is right - I did this in R
  real<lower = 0, upper = 2 * pi()> z_star[M];       // posterior predicted z
  real<lower = 0, upper = 2 * pi()> y_star[M];      // back-transformation z -> y
  real<lower = 0, upper = 2 * pi()> mu;                    // mean of y
  real<lower = 0> var_y_star;                                      // variance of y_star
  real<lower = 0> kappa_approx;                               // approximate concentration of y

  mu <- mu_z / scale_factor + min(y);
  for(m in 1:M){
    z_star[m] ~ von_mises(mu_z, kappa_z);
    y_star[m] <- z_star[m] / scale_factor + min(y);
  }
  var_y_star <- sum(pow(y_star - mu, 2)) / (M - 1);
  kappa_approx <- 1/var_y_star;                                   // kappa_approx -> kappa as kappa -> Inf

}

>

My understanding from Bob's comments is that the leapfrog tree keeps hitting it's maximum in the flat model. The tree keeps growing, because none of the simulations turn around. As the tree grows, there's a bunch of simulations to keep track off, and that's the overhead cost that makes sampling for the flat model so much more intensive than the model with weak priors.
>
> Does that sound right?

Not quite.  With flat priors your posterior mass extends from x, y = + infinity to x, y = - infinity.  In order to draw an independent sample NUTS is going to pick a direction and chug along to one of the infinities.  It would go forever but we have a the max_depth limit to avoid these issues.  With weak priors there’s only a finite region to explore and NUTS turns around quickly.

Again, it’s not that Stan is slow in the model without priors but rather that the model is ill-posed and it would take infinite time to generate an independent sample no matter what you did.  The overhead for building a bit tree is not trivial but it’s not that important.

> Thanks, gents. I get all the unidentified stuff. Every sampler handles such a model slightly differently, so it's become

> overhead cost that makes sampling for the flat model so much more intensive than the model with weak priors.
>

It's why it takes so long --- if you look at the negative log
probability it's a long valley, and Stan moves up and down it.
Moving down the valley involves many log probability and gradient
evals.  Each update in JAGS/BUGS is conjugate and only moves
a little way.  Basically, Gibbs devolves into a random walk
that barely begins to explore the improper posterior.

But, and this is the thing to keep in mind, neither Stan nor
BUGS nor JAGS is actually properly sampling from this model's
posterior, which is improper.  As Michael pointed out, values
of lambda_1 = 1e100 should be as likely as those with lambda_1 = 0.

2000 leapfrog steps.  The improper model averages 1300, which

messages.body_plain:
I have no idea how people typically do this.  There's no
good way to constrain a vector beta so that for arbitrary
vector x we have x' * beta > 0 (or x' * beta < 0).

You could always exponentiate, but that's a different link
function.  That does seem to be what R does judging from the
doc for its glm() function:

# A Gamma example, from McCullagh & Nelder (1989, pp. 300-2)
clotting <- data.frame(
     u = c(5,10,15,20,30,40,60,80,100),
     lot1 = c(118,58,42,35,27,25,21,19,18),
     lot2 = c(69,35,26,21,18,16,13,12,12))
summary(glm(lot1 ~ log(u), data=clotting, family=Gamma))
summary(glm(lot2 ~ log(u), data=clotting, family=Gamma))

- Bob

On 2/7/14, 4:05 AM, Marco Inacio wrote:
> Hi everybody. I'm intending to do a gamma regression using stan and according to what I read, the gamma distribution
> canonical link is:
>

> $\beta X = -1/\mu$  (where $\mu$ is the mean)
>
> And since $\mu = \alpha/\beta$  and $\alpha, \beta > 0$.
>
> Then $\beta X < 0$, which seems a little problematic condition.
>
> Did I got it right? If so, does Stan work fine with such limitation in the possible values of $\beta$ or do I need to
> configure it somehow, or do you just recommend me to use another kind of link function like $\beta X = log(\mu)$ which

On Fri, Feb 7, 2014 at 10:12 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> I have no idea how people typically do this.  There's no
> good way to constrain a vector beta so that for arbitrary
> vector x we have x' * beta > 0 (or x' * beta < 0).

Actually this isn't too hard to do in Stan if one of those vectors is data.  Lets say x is a fixed N dimensional data vector.  Then use something like Gram-Schmidt to find the set of N-1 unit vectors v_i which are orthogonal to x (i.e., such that dot_product(x,v_i) = 0).  Then \beta = \alpha x + \sum_i \gamma_i v_i  where the \gamma_i are unconstrained and \alpha is constrained to be negative.  It's then simple to show that \beta x will always be negative.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Yes and no.  You can generate fake data in one of
two ways:  using the generated quantities block or
parameters plus a model.  The latter is more general,
but also more costly because it's MCMC, not just MC.

There are two problems, though.  First, you have
to write the data generating model in Stan, which isn't
like the original model.  You can often do this using the
parameters approach by swapping what's data and what's
parameters.

The second problem is that the output CSV format for
Stan can't easily be fed back into Stan.  So if you then
want to iterate and fit again (as Andrew's always suggesting),
then it's not so easy.

We'll hopefully have a routine to do this soon, at which
point I'll write a chapter into the Stan manual on how to do
it from CmdStan.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I think I have good enough results using what I think of as a 1-parameter beta model, where the mean is the one parameter.
I took the original 1-4 scale and divided by 5, leaving the range from .2 through .8.  This was to avoid putting a lot of mass at the end points, since the beta doesn't like that (the manual seems  to indicate 0 and 1 are not legal values).  Then I fit a beta model parameterized by mean and "size" (courtesy of wikipedia) where the regression model applied only to the mean.  So there was a 2nd beta parameter, but it was just a single parameter rather than a fuller model.  Finally, when simulating I pull values outside of [1, 4] to the endpoints, which gives me a bit of a pile up at the end points, just like the original data.

Small syntax question: I didn't declare some variables in the model block (I just noticed it); is that a problem (see below)?

Here's the code:
data {
   int<lower=0> N; // number of respondents
   int<lower=0> J;  //number of covariates
   int<lower=0> NSD;  // number of classes of beta for sd
   int<lower=1,upper=NSD> SDClass[J];  // beta[j, k] has sigma_beta[SDClass[j]]
   int<lower=0> NCLUSTER;  //number of seeds
   int iCluster[N]; // cluster id
   matrix[N, J] x;  // covariates
   vector<lower=1,upper=4>[N] y;  // outcome
}
transformed data {
   vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] z;
   z <- y/5.0;
}
parameters {
    vector[J] beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients
    vector[NCLUSTER] alpha_raw; // cluster effects
    real<lower=0> nu; // 'size' parameter
    real<lower=0> sigma_alpha;
    real<lower=0> sigma_beta[NSD];
}
transformed parameters {
    vector[J] beta;
    vector[NCLUSTER] alpha;
    for(ir in 1:J) {
       beta[ir] <- beta_raw[ir]*sigma_beta[SDClass[ir]];
    }
    alpha <- alpha_raw*sigma_alpha;
}
model {
    vector[N] mu;
    vector[N] parm1;
    vector[N] parm2;
    nu ~ cauchy(0, 5); //maybe it should start above 0
    sigma_alpha ~ cauchy(0, 5);
    sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5);
    beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5);
    for (j in 2:J) {
      beta_raw[j] ~ normal(0, 1);
    }
    alpha_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
    for (n in 1:N) {
        mu[n] <- inv_logit((x[n] * beta)+alpha[iCluster[n]]);
    }
    parm1 <- mu*nu;
    parm2 <- (1-mu)*nu;
    z ~ beta(parm1, parm2);
}

parm1 and parm2 don't have declared data type, which seems to contradict the first sentence of section 21 of the manual.  Is that a problem?
Ross

I've been getting more of these selectChildren warnings and looked into it.
Apparently they require all of
1) using R (specifically the parallel library mclapply)
2) using Rmpi
3) using an old version of openmpi.

See
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/14149361/rmpi-mclapply-in-selectchildrenac-1-error-interrupted-system-call-in-s
for details (and the link there to the openmpi list).

older open mpi's) which produces the warnings.

They appear harmless.  And, to repeat, r/stan is a bystander to this
infelicity, not a cause.

Ross Boylan

On 2/8/14, 4:52 PM, Marco Inacio wrote:
>
>
>
> On 14-02-07 03:09 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:

>> On Fri, Feb 7, 2014 at 10:12 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
>>
>>     I have no idea how people typically do this.  There's no
>>     good way to constrain a vector beta so that for arbitrary

>>     vector $x$ we have $x' * beta > 0$ (or $x' * beta < 0$).
>>
>>
>> Actually this isn't too hard to do in Stan if one of those vectors is data.  Lets say $x$ is a fixed $N$ dimensional
>> data vector.  Then use something like Gram-Schmidt to find the set of $N-1$ unit vectors $v_i$ which are orthogonal to
>> $x$ (i.e., such that dot_product(x,v_i) = 0).  Then $\beta = \alpha x + \sum_i \gamma_i v_i$  where the $\gamma_i$ are
>> unconstrained and $\alpha$ is constrained to be negative.  It's then simple to show that $\beta x$ will always be
>> negative.
>
>
> Thanks, I wonder if there's a way to extend this to a matrix of data $x$, we could do it for each column of the matrix,
> but seems a little too strong to force every $\beta * x_i$ ($x_i$ is column $i$ of matrix $x$) to be negative instead of

> just the sum them. But no need to worry about this now, I'll prefer using log-link anyway.
>
>
> Could you please help with this other problem? I wish to know if need to add Jacobian here in this case 'cause this
> model is taking more than 10 hours for just 100 iterations with very low number of n_eff.

I don't understand the model, but here are some suggestions and
questions.

Given that log(sigma) shows up, you almost certainly want to be
defining sigma with a lower bound,

   real<lower=0> sigma;

The constraints declared on variables needs to match their support
in the model.

Add a Jacobian for what?   You only need a Jacobian adjustment
for a change of variables.

I take it in increment_log_prob(sum(summands)) that
each summand is supposed to be a gamma distribution?

lgamma() is very expensive to evaluate, so if the loop is large,
this is going to be slow.

You want to define a local variable log_sigma =log(sigma)
rather than continually recomputing it.

Unless you want to inspect all those transformed parameters
in the output, you can just make them local variables in the
model.

exp(log(a) - b) is more efficiently coded as a * exp(-b)
as long as exp(-b) won't overflow or underflow.

exp(2*(eta1[i] - log(sigma)))

   = square(exp(eta1[i] - log(sigma)))

   = square(-sigma * exp(eta1[i])

   = square(-sigma) * square(exp(eta1[i]])

and now you can just save square(-sigma) and reuse it
rather than recomputing it.  Same for exp(eta1[i])
which gets reused in the summands.

You define eta0 and zeta1 but don't use them.  This
is expensive in Stan because it causes unused derivative
evaluation and chain-rule propagations.

It won't make much difference to speed in this model, but you
don't need to build up summands or alpha as vectors.
You can make them locals in the loop and just increment_log_prob()
for each of what is now summands[i] --- increment_log_prob()
automatically vectorizes its sums internally.  Just define the
terms you reuse (log(sigma) and square(-sigma)) as locals outside
the loop.

Why is there a final increment_log_prob(-log(sigma)); ?

Part of the computational problem may be overly vague priors:

  beta ~ normal(0, 100);
   gamma ~ normal(0, 100);

If you don't expect beta or gamma to be in the 100s, don't use
priors this wide.

In general, though, I'd suggest you get the model working before trying
to optimize too heavily.  Then inspect what's going on with the samples
and see if the parameters are identified or if they need tighter priors.

- Bob

Hi Matus,

This is the first time I've seen this error. Thanks for reporting it. Are you
using Linux?

I'm not sure how one can debug this error but I do have a suggestion that might
fix it. If you just set a random seed each time you call `sampling` it's
possible everything will work (it's also not a bad idea in general). For
example,

    fit = sm.sampling(data=dat,iter=1000,chains=4,warmup=200,thin=2,n_jobs=2, seed=5)

If the error still occurs, please post the seed you are using.

Best wishes,

-a

based on the time like we do in RStan?   It seems awkward to
have to have users alwyas set seeds.

if it's generated randomly, so that users can reproduce their
results and we can help them debug issues.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

I'm not sure about this error. I wonder if it might have arisen via a mismatch
between some compiled thing (libstan.a or a Cython extension). Naturally I'll
revisit this judgement if someone else has the problem. Fixing the seed was my
band-aid solution.

Just like RStan, PyStan does save the seed that is used -- but we can only get
access to this seed if the sampler completes and returns a fit object.

Best,

-a

messages.subject: Re: Transitioning to Stan
messages.subject_clean: Transitioning to Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Kevin.  I'm ccing the Stan-users list as they might have some thoughts.
For my collaborators in political science, Stan has been most useful for models where the data set is not huge (e.g., we might have 10,000 data points or 50,000 data points but not 10 million) but where the model is somewhat complex (for example, a model with latent time series structure).  The point is that the model has enough parameters and uncertainty that you'll want to do full Bayes (rather than some sort of point estimate).  At that point, Stan is a winner compared to programming one's own Monte Carlo algorithm.
I hope this helps.
Andrew

On Feb 11, 2014, at 7:09 PM, Kevin Cartier wrote:

> Hello Andrew:
>
> I've been happily using R for a number of years now and recently came across Stan. Looks big and powerful, so I'd like to pick an appropriate project and try it out. I wondered if you could point me to a link or document that goes into the motivation for this tool (aside from the Stan user doc)?  What I'd like to understand is, at what point might you look at an emergent R project and advise, "You know, that thing you're trying to do would be a whole lot easier/simpler/more straightforward to implement with Stan." (or words to that effect).
>
> Any recommendation you can provide would be much appreciated,
>
> Sincerely,
>
> Kevin C. Cartier
> Cleveland, Ohio
>
>

Hi Bob,

re: the seed -- if you glance at the reported error, Python is telling us it got
passed something wacky as a seed and it is giving up. My thinking was that if
the user provides an integer as a seed then Python (or whatever) will not
provide a wacky one.

I still think this is likely a mismatch between compiled objects -- i.e.,
there's a compiled Cython extension that's maybe version 2.0 and libstan is 2.1
or something like that. In this particular case, I'm OK with a band-aid solution
since it seems next to impossible to debug without access to the affected
filesystem.

Best,

-a

messages.body_plain: I notice that there is no mention of the Zipf distribution in the Stan user's manual. Is it possible to approximate this distribution by any transformation of a differently distributed random variable?
messages.body_snippet: I notice that there is no mention of the Zipf distribution in the Stan user's manual. Is it possible to approximate this distribution by any transformation of a differently distributed random variable

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Zipf distribution
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Zipf distribution
messages.body_plain:
It's easy to implement for a fixed power (see the chapter on
implementing custom probability functions), but we don't have
the Riemann zeta function implemented (yet), so it's not possible to do it
for varying parameters.

If you can deal with a continous approximation, there's the Pareto
distribution in Stan.

Boost provides Riemann zeta,

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_55_0/libs/math/doc/html/math_toolkit/zetas/zeta.html

messages.subject: Transformation for Interval-Censored Disease Incidence Data
messages.subject_clean: Transformation for Interval-Censored Disease Incidence Data
messages.body_plain:
Hi -

I was wondering if anyone could help me out with the following problem:

I have data from an outbreak of an infectious disease, with, for example, the following number of new cases observed on each successive day of  the outbreak, i.e. Day 1: 1 case, Day 2: 2 cases, Day 3: 3 cases, Day 4: 0 cases.

The problem is that the model I would like to fit to the data is a continuous time model, but the onset times for these cases are interval-censored and reported as the day in which the case reported symptoms. So, at t=0, we're at the very beginning of the first day, etc.  This means that an individual who reported illness on day 2 could have become ill at any point on day 2, i.e. at t = 1.75, etc.

This can be dealt with easily by assuming a uniform prior on the onset times for each case and modeling the latent onset time as a real variable on the range from [d-1, d], where d is the day of reporting. The problem with this is that on days where there are multiple case reports (i.e. most of them), we throw out a potentially important piece of information, which is that these latent onset times also follow some unobserved order, i.e. case 1 must have had onset before case 2, even if they were both reported on day 2.

At present, I am modeling these onset times as a vector of reals on the range from [0,1] and then adding this value to (d-1) to get the unobserved onset time. My question is whether there's a way to leverage the type of approach used to create unbounded ordered and positive ordered vectors in Stan to create ordered vectors on some bounded interval.

Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

thanks,
Jon Zelner

messages.subject: Re: functions and ODEs in Stan --- design docs
messages.subject_clean: functions and ODEs in Stan --- design docs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

We (a group of pharmacometricians at Metrum Research Group) have been exploring the use of stan as an alternative to other tools (BUGS, JAGS, NONMEM, ..). We are particularly interested in the proposed addition of ODE solvers to stan and their use for pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PKPD) data analysis. Here are a few comments on the “ODE Integrator Support” page on the stan wiki (https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/ODE-Integrator-Support). This input is informed in part by my experience developing the bugsModelLibrary add-on for WinBUGS.

“The only robust solution to dosing is to integrate between dosings. This would, of course, require a more complicated input, with dose times and a delta for the state for each dose time.”

> We concur with this approach to dealing with dosing events, but we would prefer to extend the approach to all inter-event intervals where “event” refers to dosing and observation events. Intermediate user-specified events might also be included. This permits parameters that vary with time as a piecewise constant function. This is the approach used in NONMEM’s PREDPP library and bugsModelLibrary. NONMEM and bugsModelLibrary also provide good examples for how you might structure the arguments for stan function calls. The approach is flexible and has the benefit of already being familiar to a large fraction of pharmacometricians who might wish to use stan for pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic modeling.

“Dosing Convenience Methods: steady-state dosing (i.e. dosing at a fixed time interval) and multiple dosing specifications (i.e. one only states “I want 50 dosing events with a between-dose time of 8h and a certain amount”). Both situations frequently arise in PK modeling and can be handled analytically very efficiently.”

> Non-steady-state multiple dosing of equal doses at equal time intervals is certainly a simple book-keeping matter of introducing a sequence of new dosing events. The steady-state case is another story. You could use brute force, i.e., simulate a large number of doses until apparent steady-state is achieved. A more efficient approach (usually) is to treat this as a boundary value ODE problem. In other words use a numerical root solver to solve for the initial conditions that result in steady-state.

Finally we encourage you to implement the ODE support in stages. Stage 1 would implement a simple ODE solver. Support for dosing and other events could be implemented in subsequent stages. This is because the stan language is sufficiently flexible that the user can write stan code that implements dosing and observation (and other) events and call the ODE solver for each inter-event interval. Thus having a simple ODE solver is sufficient for most PKPD modeling problems albeit not as convenient or efficient as having the event schedule handled by built-in code.

The attached zip file contains R and stan code that illustrates user-written code for such recursive calculations. In this case it uses the analytical solution for a linear 2 compartment model with 1st order absorption, but you can imagine that a call to a numerical ODE solver could replace the analytic calculations.

Thanks for all the stan team's efforts in developing such a flexible analysis platform.

Bill Gillespie

messages.subject: Useful trick for compiling Stan models with debug info
messages.subject_clean: Useful trick for compiling Stan models with debug info
messages.body_plain:
There is no obvious way, using the Stan make files, to compile a model with debug info so that you can run it under gdb. You can, of course, use make -n to see the commands that will be run and then modify them to include the -g flag, but that's a bit awkward. The make files do, however, allow you to explicitly set the optimization level; for example, you can do

    make O=0 <path to my model with .stan extension removed>

As a hack, you can sneak a -g flag in there:

    make O="0 -g" <path to my model with .stan extension removed>

On Windows, you'll have to use O="1 -g", as an optimization level of 0 causes problems compiling.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can 3pl Item Response Theory model be estimated in Stan?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Can 3pl Item Response Theory model be estimated in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
It should be possible to estimate 3PL in Stan.  At least
as possible in any other Bayesian estimation.

What kinds of problems are you having?  If you send us the model,
we might be able to help.

The 3PL problem does introduce another degree of freedom at
the item level and it should correlate negatively with
item difficulty in the posterior, because there are now two
ways to account for a lot of students getting it right, either
an easy problem or an easy problem to guess.  So you're almost
certainly going to need reasonable priors if you don't have
a lot of data, especially if you have problems that almost
every student got right (if they all got them wrong, it's not
such an issue, because the guessing rate is bounded below at zero).

So I'd suggest looking at a hierarchical model with covariance among
the three item-level parameters, guessing rate, difficulty, and discrimination.

- Bob
