messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] custom probabilities - normalization - slow
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] custom probabilities - normalization - slow
messages.body_plain:
On Feb 21, 2014, at 5:26 PM, Ulrike Schlägel <ulrike.s...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi,
>
> I've recently started to try out Stan, after having speed problems with JAGS. Still, I run into the same with Stan, so I was wondering if there's someone out there who could point me in a direction how to speed up things - or tell me that my models are just not suitable for Stan.
>
> I model time series as Markov processes. At each time step, the random variable y_t is a sample of a finite number of possible outcomes, say {1,...,M}. The probability mass function of y_t changes at each time step and is a function involving some standard density functions and a custom function based on covariates. Something like this
> y_t | y_{t-1}  ~  some_density(y_t; y_{t-1}) * custom_function(y_t; covariates) / normalization_constant
> The likelihood is the product of all those pieces for the entire time series.
>
> The problem is the normalization constant. For each time step, it is the sum of the numerator evaluated for all possible outcomes {1,...,M}, and it involves the model parameters, so cannot just be ignored as a constant. This sum has to be calculated for each time step.
>
> I run into the problem that if M (number of possible outcomes at each step) and N (number of time steps in time series) are large, say M=400, N=1000, calculating the normlization constant slows the sampling down a lot.
>
> I was hoping that Stan would be better suited to this than JAGS, because it compiles a C++ code. If I do similar calculations (summing to obtain the normalization constants) just in C++, it is simple and fast. So I am wondering whether the implementation of summing is somehow time consuming in Stan, or whether it's the calculation of gradients, or something else.

Yes, it's the gradients that slow down the sum.  Calculating sums in Stan is just as
fast as in C++ -- it just reduces to the obvious C++ analogue.  But calculating
gradients builds up the whole expression tree in memory for the sum then propagates
derivatives backward with the chain rule in a second pass.

But this might not be why sampling is slow.

When you say it's fast in C++, you mean you have a sampler written in C++ that
gets good effective sample sizes per second?  If so, what sampling algorithm are
you using?

> I'd be very grateful if someone would comment on this. Any help and info is appreciated.
>
> I've made a little fake example of the model type that I'm trying to fit that has the speed problems. I am attaching 2 versions of stan model formulations that I tried. "fakeCustom.stan" uses increment_log_prob() to manually specify the log-likelihood. "fakeCategorial.stan" uses a categorical distribution for each y_t - using categorical_logit to normalize the probabilities. I also tried categorical in combination with softmax(), but that didn't improve things.
> I am also attaching R dump files with fake data for both stan models. For this data, I used M=50 and N=100. This is much lower than what I really need, but this is more suitable for demonstration (because possible to run). After compiling the model, running just 100 iterations takes a few minutes with both model versions. For M=few hundred, N=1000, it would take much longer.
> It tried both using Stan via command line and rstan. For rstan, I also attach files that are capable of producing the fake data and fit the models via stan().

Looking at your fakeCustom file, you can define

  log_weight[n] <- log_inv_logit(...)

and use that rather than log(weight[n]) because

  log_inv_logit(u) =def= log(inv_logit(u))

with

  inv_logit(u) =def= 1 / (1 + exp(-u))

There is also a much faster and more arithmetically stable
function

  log_sum_exp(v) = log(sum(exp(v))

So this:

        for (i in 1:M)
            normpiece[i] <- exp(-square(x[i]-y[n-1])/(2*square(sigma))) / (1+exp(-alpha-beta1*res1[n,i]-beta2*res2[n,i]));
        norm <- sum(normpiece);

        ... log(norm) ...

can be replaced with

        for (i in 1:M)
            log_normpiece[i] <- -square(x[i]-y[n-1])/(2*square(sigma))) / (1+exp(-alpha-beta1*res1[n,i]-beta2*res2[n,i]);
        log_norm <- log_sum_exp(log_normpiece);

        ... log_norm ...

where again the 1/(1 + exp(-u)) bit can be replaced with inv_logit(u).

So your two blocks would look something like:

transformed parameters {
    real<lower=0, upper=1> log_weight[N];
    for (n in 1:N)
      log_weight[n] <- log_inv_logit(-alpha - beta1 * cov1[n] - beta2 * cov2[n]);
}
model {
    real log_norm;
    real square_sigma;
    vector[M] log_normpiece;
    square_sigma <- square(sigma);
    for (n in 2:N) {
        for (i in 1:M)
          normpiece[i]
            <- -square(x[i] - y[n-1]) / (2*square(sigma))
            + log_inv_logit(alpha - beta1 * res1[n,i]- beta2 * res2[n,i]);
        log_norm <- log_sum_exp(log_normpiece);
        increment_log_prob( (-0.5) * square(y[n] - y[n-1]) / square_sigma
                            + log_weight[n] - log_norm );
    }
}

You should check my algebra here --- you had lots of brackets floating around.
Note that I also changed - u / 2 to (- 0.5) * u, which replaces a negation and
division with a single multiplication.

All of this will only make the iterations faster --- it won't help at
all with effective sample size if that's your issue.

Is it sampling properly, just slowly?

You don't need to go back to Stan 2.1.0 --- the issue was with Rcpp.
But we've worked around the install issues for that, too.  Not that
it'll make any difference for this problem.

- Bob

On Sunday, February 23, 2014 12:53:29 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> That's good news for people who want to use Coda.
>
> I'm more interested in going the other way around and
> letting us analyze BUGS and JAGS output using RStan's posterior
> analysis tools so we can do the comparisons Andrew wants to do
> using the new split R-hat and n_eff calcs.  Is that also easy?

The monitor() function already exists in RStan. You just need an array whose dimensions are

simulations x chains x parameters

but coda (and the rest of the world) is inclined to think in terms of

simulations x parameters x chains

so you need

mcmc.list2array <-
  function(x) {
    stopifnot(class(x)[1] != "mcmc.list")
    arr <- array(NA_real_,
                 dim = c(nrow(x[[1]]), length(x), ncol(x[[1]])))
    dimnames(arr)[[3]] <- colnames(x[[1]])
    for(i in seq_along(x)) arr[,i,] <- as.matrix(x[[i]])
    return(arr)
  }

Ben

> > #include "stdafx.h"

Yes it is minimal... Now, at least I am sure I can compile a program including stan.hpp.

I probably build gtest and run the existing tests, or hopefully someone gives me a test program :)

Here is my little notes:
1.compile libstan.lib using visual studio

To do this,
1.0 change the platform to x64(simply because I had a bad experience with 32bit in g++).
1.1 In properties, Include boost_1.54.0, eigen_3.2.0, and stan headers which come along with the source codes of stan.
1.2 move src\stan\agrad\rev\ver_stack.hpp and src\stan\agrad\rev\ver_stack.cpp to your build directory.
1.3 then build the project with debug and release mode, which creates new folder x64. which contains Debug and Release folders. Inside them, you find libstan.lib

2.compile stan program
To do this,
2.0 start new empty console program and change the platform to x64.
2.1 In properties, Include boost_1.54.0, eigen_3.2.0, and stan headers which come along with the source codes of stan.
2.2 In properties, add library directories where they have libstan.lib for debug and release modes.
2.3 In properties, In linker, there should add libstan.lib in additional dependencies.
2.4 then you can build debug and release mode :)

3. test a simple stan program
I am here.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Stéphane,

The warning is quite explicit: the matrix failed the positive definite test by a really really small number. This is a pretty common problem with priors on multivariate distribution.

A good exercise in frustration with this problem is to try to sample from a multivariate distribution with the package MASS in R with what you believe to be a positive-definite symmetric covariance matrix. Most often than not the matrix is not exactly positive-definite and you will have to thinker with it with and use a function like make.positive.definite() from the package corpcor to coerce the function to work.

As stated in the message itself this is not a serious problem unless you see the message really frequently. The message will invariably appear a few time right after you initialized the model, it will probably pop up randomly during the adaptation phase. It should have disappeared completely by the time you reach the sampling stage.

As far as your second question is concerned all models will be slower in stan compared to jags. I believe this is even more apparent for multivariate models. I'm pretty sure the manual had a section on this part at some point although I haven't read the newer versions.

However, and this is really important, for simple models stan will converge more quickly and will produce a higher number of effective sample sizes. As far as my experience with more complex models the advantage of stan over jags is that the model will ultimately converge... something I never achieved with jags.

Chris
------------

messages.body_plain:
As Chris noted, you have to be careful with your comparisons.  Is the time per sample much larger,
or the time per _effective_ sample?  Only the latter matters for efficient inference.

If you are seeing larger times per effective sample then you may be running into issues with the
Wishart prior.  Outside of conjugate models Wishart priors are notorious for inducing heavy tailed
posteriors which become difficult to fit.  Be aware that WinBUGS and JAGS aren’t necessarily
fitting them correctly, either, the Gibbs samplers they use are just less expressive to such
pathologies.

Hi Bob,

Thank you very much for looking at my problem and suggesting more efficient formulations!

I've tried out your suggestions, and using the log_sum_exp() instead of a straightforward sum did make the sampling a little bit faster. Still, I ran a test with higher dimensions and sample size (time series length N=1000, number of possible outcomes of each step M=225), and a run with 100 iterations took 1.5 hours. So it seems to me that just the sampling is already slow, without even thinking yet about effective sample size.

So HMC is maybe not the best method for my model type?

Thanks a lot again for taking the time to look at my model and your help.

Uli

On Friday, 21 February 2014 21:07:39 UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> On Feb 21, 2014, at 5:26 PM, Ulrike Schlägel <ulrike.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Hi,
> >
> > I've recently started to try out Stan, after having speed problems with JAGS. Still, I run into the same with Stan, so I was wondering if there's someone out there who could point me in a direction how to speed up things - or tell me that my models are just not suitable for Stan.
> >
> > I model time series as Markov processes. At each time step, the random variable y_t is a sample of a finite number of possible outcomes, say {1,...,M}. The probability mass function of y_t changes at each time step and is a function involving some standard density functions and a custom function based on covariates. Something like this
> > y_t | y_{t-1}  ~  some_density(y_t; y_{t-1}) * custom_function(y_t; covariates) / normalization_constant
> > The likelihood is the product of all those pieces for the entire time series.
> >
> > The problem is the normalization constant. For each time step, it is the sum of the numerator evaluated for all possible outcomes {1,...,M}, and it involves the model parameters, so cannot just be ignored as a constant. This sum has to be calculated for each time step.
> >
> > I run into the problem that if M (number of possible outcomes at each step) and N (number of time steps in time series) are large, say M=400, N=1000, calculating the normlization constant slows the sampling down a lot.
> >
> > I was hoping that Stan would be better suited to this than JAGS, because it compiles a C++ code. If I do similar calculations (summing to obtain the normalization constants) just in C++, it is simple and fast. So I am wondering whether the implementation of summing is somehow time consuming in Stan, or whether it's the calculation of gradients, or something else.
>
> Yes, it's the gradients that slow down the sum.  Calculating sums in Stan is just as
> fast as in C++ -- it just reduces to the obvious C++ analogue.  But calculating
> gradients builds up the whole expression tree in memory for the sum then propagates
> derivatives backward with the chain rule in a second pass.
>
> But this might not be why sampling is slow.
>
> When you say it's fast in C++, you mean you have a sampler written in C++ that
> gets good effective sample sizes per second?  If so, what sampling algorithm are
> you using?
>
>
> > I'd be very grateful if someone would comment on this. Any help and info is appreciated.
> >
> > I've made a little fake example of the model type that I'm trying to fit that has the speed problems. I am attaching 2 versions of stan model formulations that I tried. "fakeCustom.stan" uses increment_log_prob() to manually specify the log-likelihood. "fakeCategorial.stan" uses a categorical distribution for each y_t - using categorical_logit to normalize the probabilities. I also tried categorical in combination with softmax(), but that didn't improve things.
> > I am also attaching R dump files with fake data for both stan models. For this data, I used M=50 and N=100. This is much lower than what I really need, but this is more suitable for demonstration (because possible to run). After compiling the model, running just 100 iterations takes a few minutes with both model versions. For M=few hundred, N=1000, it would take much longer.
> > It tried both using Stan via command line and rstan. For rstan, I also attach files that are capable of producing the fake data and fit the models via stan().
>
> Looking at your fakeCustom file, you can define
>
>   log_weight[n] <- log_inv_logit(...)
>
> and use that rather than log(weight[n]) because
>
>   log_inv_logit(u) =def= log(inv_logit(u))
>
> with
>
>   inv_logit(u) =def= 1 / (1 + exp(-u))
>
> There is also a much faster and more arithmetically stable
> function
>
>   log_sum_exp(v) = log(sum(exp(v))
>
> So this:
>
>         for (i in 1:M)
>             normpiece[i] <- exp(-square(x[i]-y[n-1])/(2*square(sigma))) / (1+exp(-alpha-beta1*res1[n,i]-beta2*res2[n,i]));
>         norm <- sum(normpiece);
>
>         ... log(norm) ...
>
> can be replaced with
>
>         for (i in 1:M)
>             log_normpiece[i] <- -square(x[i]-y[n-1])/(2*square(sigma))) / (1+exp(-alpha-beta1*res1[n,i]-beta2*res2[n,i]);
>         log_norm <- log_sum_exp(log_normpiece);
>
>         ... log_norm ...
>
> where again the 1/(1 + exp(-u)) bit can be replaced with inv_logit(u).
>
> So your two blocks would look something like:
>
> transformed parameters {
>     real<lower=0, upper=1> log_weight[N];
>     for (n in 1:N)
>       log_weight[n] <- log_inv_logit(-alpha - beta1 * cov1[n] - beta2 * cov2[n]);
> }
> model {
>     real log_norm;
>     real square_sigma;
>     vector[M] log_normpiece;
>     square_sigma <- square(sigma);
>     for (n in 2:N) {
>         for (i in 1:M)
>           normpiece[i]
>             <- -square(x[i] - y[n-1]) / (2*square(sigma))
>             + log_inv_logit(alpha - beta1 * res1[n,i]- beta2 * res2[n,i]);
>         log_norm <- log_sum_exp(log_normpiece);
>         increment_log_prob( (-0.5) * square(y[n] - y[n-1]) / square_sigma
>                             + log_weight[n] - log_norm );
>     }

messages.body_plain:
>  About the slowness, I mean the total time, obtained by system.time(sampling(......)).

Yeah, that’s not particularly helpful here.  HMC iterations take longer but yield MUCH
higher effective sample sizes and hence more efficient MCMC.

> I have chosen to try a model with a covariance matrix because I have seen that Stan allows prior distributions other than the Wishart distribution. I'd like to compare the different priors.

Absolutely, that’s one of the great use cases for Stan and the LKJ priors are awesome.

> Actually I used this model on real data when I was a WinBUGS user, and I remember the convergence was not clearly achieved.

It can be even more insidious than that as the chains might appear to have converged but still
be highly biased due to ergodicity issues.  I’d recommend at least confirming that your model
gets the right answers with simulated data.

Good luck.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow sampling and "WW is not positive definite" in wishart_log
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Slow sampling and "WW is not positive definite" in wishart_log
messages.body_plain:
For (1), those are informational messages you can ignore if they
don't happen very often.  You often see them in warmup until adaptation
has converged to a decent step size.  It just indicates a Metropolis
rejection.  The source is typically arithmetic issues with too large
step sizes in the discretization of the simulation of the Hamiltonian
dynamics in the HMC algorithm.

We're going to remove the message because it's been confusing our users.
We haven't been able to stress its informational nature enough to
stop worrying people.

For (2), are you sure you're getting the same answers from JAGS and Stan,
especially in terms of posterior variance?

If I'm remembering JAGS correctly, I don't think the JAGS and Stan
are identitcal.  Stan uses covariance as its parameterization of
multi_normal, whereas I think JAGS uses precision matrices.  So you
either want to use Stan's multi_normal_prec() or use the inverse Wishart
with appropriate priors.  You can also make it even faster by
Cholesky factoring the covariance matrix outside of the loop
and using multi_normal_cholesky() within the loop instead of plain multi_normal().
See page 96 of the 2.2.0 manual.

Having said that, we have alternative recommendations
for priors at the end of the regression chapter that we think make more sense.
You can't code them in JAGS/BUGS because they're not conjugate, but they let
you shrink toward identity correlation (or take a uniform distribution on correlation)
and then have independently scales by dimension.

Stan can also be much more efficient at exploring fat tails and also at uncovering
what's effectively non-identifiability in the model.  See the new manual
chapter on problematic posteriors.

Also for (2), are you measuring effective samples per second rather than just
iteration speed?   Only the number of effective samples matters for inferences.
Often Stan has slower iterations, but better mixing.

We wouldn't recommend a normal(0,1000) prior unless you really expect your
Mu to be that huge.  Again, see the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual
for more info.

Finally, how are you initializing in both systems and what does the
number of iterations to convergence look like?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Do other samplers run faster and get the right answer?

If you get 20 or 30 effective samples with 100 iterations,
that may be all you need --- it's all you need for most MCMC
inference.

- Bob

On Feb 24, 2014, at 7:47 PM, Ulrike Schlägel <ulrike.s...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Bob,
>
> Thank you very much for looking at my problem and suggesting more efficient formulations!
>
> I've tried out your suggestions, and using the log_sum_exp() instead of a straightforward sum did make the sampling a little bit faster. Still, I ran a test with higher dimensions and sample size (time series length N=1000, number of possible outcomes of each step M=225), and a run with 100 iterations took 1.5 hours. So it seems to me that just the sampling is already slow, without even thinking yet about effective sample size.
>
> So HMC is maybe not the best method for my model type?
>
> Thanks a lot again for taking the time to look at my model and your help.
>
> Uli
>
>
> On Friday, 21 February 2014 21:07:39 UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> On Feb 21, 2014, at 5:26 PM, Ulrike Schlägel <ulrike.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Hi,
> >
> > I've recently started to try out Stan, after having speed problems with JAGS. Still, I run into the same with Stan, so I was wondering if there's someone out there who could point me in a direction how to speed up things - or tell me that my models are just not suitable for Stan.
> >
> > I model time series as Markov processes. At each time step, the random variable y_t is a sample of a finite number of possible outcomes, say {1,...,M}. The probability mass function of y_t changes at each time step and is a function involving some standard density functions and a custom function based on covariates. Something like this
> > y_t | y_{t-1}  ~  some_density(y_t; y_{t-1}) * custom_function(y_t; covariates) / normalization_constant
> > The likelihood is the product of all those pieces for the entire time series.
> >
> > The problem is the normalization constant. For each time step, it is the sum of the numerator evaluated for all possible outcomes {1,...,M}, and it involves the model parameters, so cannot just be ignored as a constant. This sum has to be calculated for each time step.
> >
> > I run into the problem that if M (number of possible outcomes at each step) and N (number of time steps in time series) are large, say M=400, N=1000, calculating the normlization constant slows the sampling down a lot.
> >
> > I was hoping that Stan would be better suited to this than JAGS, because it compiles a C++ code. If I do similar calculations (summing to obtain the normalization constants) just in C++, it is simple and fast. So I am wondering whether the implementation of summing is somehow time consuming in Stan, or whether it's the calculation of gradients, or something else.
>
> Yes, it's the gradients that slow down the sum.  Calculating sums in Stan is just as
> fast as in C++ -- it just reduces to the obvious C++ analogue.  But calculating
> gradients builds up the whole expression tree in memory for the sum then propagates
> derivatives backward with the chain rule in a second pass.
>
> But this might not be why sampling is slow.
>
> When you say it's fast in C++, you mean you have a sampler written in C++ that
> gets good effective sample sizes per second?  If so, what sampling algorithm are
> you using?
>
>
> > I'd be very grateful if someone would comment on this. Any help and info is appreciated.
> >
> > I've made a little fake example of the model type that I'm trying to fit that has the speed problems. I am attaching 2 versions of stan model formulations that I tried. "fakeCustom.stan" uses increment_log_prob() to manually specify the log-likelihood. "fakeCategorial.stan" uses a categorical distribution for each y_t - using categorical_logit to normalize the probabilities. I also tried categorical in combination with softmax(), but that didn't improve things.
> > I am also attaching R dump files with fake data for both stan models. For this data, I used M=50 and N=100. This is much lower than what I really need, but this is more suitable for demonstration (because possible to run). After compiling the model, running just 100 iterations takes a few minutes with both model versions. For M=few hundred, N=1000, it would take much longer.
> > It tried both using Stan via command line and rstan. For rstan, I also attach files that are capable of producing the fake data and fit the models via stan().
>
> Looking at your fakeCustom file, you can define
>
>   log_weight[n] <- log_inv_logit(...)
>
> and use that rather than log(weight[n]) because
>
>   log_inv_logit(u) =def= log(inv_logit(u))
>
> with
>
>   inv_logit(u) =def= 1 / (1 + exp(-u))
>
> There is also a much faster and more arithmetically stable
> function
>
>   log_sum_exp(v) = log(sum(exp(v))
>
> So this:
>
>         for (i in 1:M)
>             normpiece[i] <- exp(-square(x[i]-y[n-1])/(2*square(sigma))) / (1+exp(-alpha-beta1*res1[n,i]-beta2*res2[n,i]));
>         norm <- sum(normpiece);
>
>         ... log(norm) ...
>
> can be replaced with
>
>         for (i in 1:M)
>             log_normpiece[i] <- -square(x[i]-y[n-1])/(2*square(sigma))) / (1+exp(-alpha-beta1*res1[n,i]-beta2*res2[n,i]);
>         log_norm <- log_sum_exp(log_normpiece);
>
>         ... log_norm ...
>
> where again the 1/(1 + exp(-u)) bit can be replaced with inv_logit(u).
>
> So your two blocks would look something like:
>
> transformed parameters {
>     real<lower=0, upper=1> log_weight[N];
>     for (n in 1:N)
>       log_weight[n] <- log_inv_logit(-alpha - beta1 * cov1[n] - beta2 * cov2[n]);
> }
> model {
>     real log_norm;
>     real square_sigma;
>     vector[M] log_normpiece;
>     square_sigma <- square(sigma);
>     for (n in 2:N) {
>         for (i in 1:M)
>           normpiece[i]
>             <- -square(x[i] - y[n-1]) / (2*square(sigma))
>             + log_inv_logit(alpha - beta1 * res1[n,i]- beta2 * res2[n,i]);
>         log_norm <- log_sum_exp(log_normpiece);
>         increment_log_prob( (-0.5) * square(y[n] - y[n-1]) / square_sigma
>                             + log_weight[n] - log_norm );
>     }
> }
>
> You should check my algebra here --- you had lots of brackets floating around.
> Note that I also changed - u / 2 to (- 0.5) * u, which replaces a negation and
> division with a single multiplication.
>
> All of this will only make the iterations faster --- it won't help at
> all with effective sample size if that's your issue.
>
> Is it sampling properly, just slowly?
>
> You don't need to go back to Stan 2.1.0 --- the issue was with Rcpp.
> But we've worked around the install issues for that, too.  Not that
> it'll make any difference for this problem.
>
> - Bob
>
> >
> > Here's my session info
> > > sessionInfo()
> > R version 3.0.2 (2013-09-25)
> > Platform: x86_64-apple-darwin10.8.0 (64-bit)
> >
> > locale:
> > [1] en_CA.UTF-8/en_CA.UTF-8/en_CA.UTF-8/C/en_CA.UTF-8/en_CA.UTF-8
> >
> > attached base packages:
> > [1] stats     graphics  grDevices utils     datasets  methods   base
> >
> > other attached packages:
> > [1] rstan_2.1.0   inline_0.3.13 Rcpp_0.10.6
> >
> > loaded via a namespace (and not attached):
> > [1] codetools_0.2-8 stats4_3.0.2    tools_3.0.2
> >
> > I don't have the latest rstan and Rcpp version, because I ran into trouble with those on my computer and found a thread in this mailing list that recommended going back to rstan 2.1.0 and Rcpp 0.10.6.
> >
> > I hope my model description makes sense. Sorry for the long post.
> >
> > Thanks for any help!
> >
> > Uli
> >

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Formulating error in covariates logistic regression model in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Stan is not R, especially when it comes to matrix slicing and dicing.
Please see the “row” and “col” functions in the manual.

Also, watch out on the beta priors — Stan uses N(mu, sigma) so for
an equivalent model you’ll want normal(0, 10).  Additionally, the
priors can be vectorized — just replace the loop with
beta ~ normal(0, 10).  Lastly, bernoulli_logit() will perform much
better than bernoulli(inv_logit()).

> Hi there,
>
> I'm trying to recode a former openbugs project in stan, so far unsuccessfuly. The background is the following: I have a binary response (Y), and a O predictors associated with my response measured with error for N observations. In my particular data setting, I know exactly the values that the covariate vector may take. The BUGS model for this data is:
>
> model {
>         for (i in 1:N) {
>                 Y[i]~dbern (p[i])
>                 p[i] <- 1/(1+exp(-z[i]))
>                 z[i] <- betas[1]+betas[2]*env1[i]+betas[3]*env2[i]+betas[4]*env1sq[i]
>                 env1[i] <- env1Table[i,k[i]]
>                 env2[i] <- env2Table[i,k[i]]
>                 env1sq[i] <- env1sqTable[i,k[i]]
>                 k[i]~dcat(pcatTable[i,])
>         }
>         betas[1] ~ dnorm(0,0.01)
>         betas[2] ~ dnorm(0,0.01)
>         betas[3] ~ dnorm(0,0.01)
>         betas[4] ~ dnorm(0,0.01)
> }
>
> My translation of this model to Stan is:
>
> logistic.cauchy.error<-'data {
>   int<lower=0> N; // number of sites
>   int<lower=0> M; // number of possible covariate vector values per site
>   int<lower=0> O; // number of regression coefficients
>   matrix[N,M] env1Table; // predictor env1matrix. Rows are observations.
>   matrix[N,M] env2Table; // predictor env2matrix. Rows are observations.
>   matrix[N,M] env1sqTable; // predictor env1sq matrix. Rows are observations.
>   matrix[N,M] pcatTable; // predictor probabilities matrix. Rows are observations.
>   int<lower=0,upper=1> Y[N];// response vector
> }
> parameters {
>   real beta[O];
>   real k[N];
> }
> model {
>   for (j in 1:O)
>     beta[j] ~ normal(0,100);
>   for (n in 1:N)
>     k[n] ~ categorical(pcatTable[n,1:M]);
>     env1[n] <- env1Table[n,k[n]];
>     env2[n] <- env2Table[n,k[n]];
>     env1sq[n] <- env1sqTable[n,k[n]];
>     Y[n] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(beta[1]+beta[2]*env1[i]+beta[3]*env2[i]+beta[4]*env1sq[i]));
> }'
>
> However, after trying to fit this model I get the error:
>
> EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=21, column=37
>
>     k[n] ~ categorical(pcatTable[n,1:M]);
>                                     ^-- here
>
>
> DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
> Parser expecting: "]"
>
> It seems I'm not properly indexing the pcatTable matrix, or in any case that pcatTable[n,1:M] is not read as a vector. Any clues on how to fix this?
>
> Thanks!
>
> Jorge Velásquez

Hi Jorge,

I think you would be better off to declare pcatTable as vector:

vector[M] pcatTable[N];

or use the row and col function to properly call the pcatTable matrix.

you might want to check the example in the manual that are using the categorical models.

Chris

messages.body_plain:
dnorm(0,.01) in BUGS is normal(0,10) in Stan.  BugS
uses precision and Stan uses standard deviation.

You use a variable "i" in the loop that's not in scope.

pcatTable[n,1:M] can be pcatTable[n] in Stan (or you can
use the row() function if you think that's clearer).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Feb 24, 2014, at 6:29 PM, Christian Roy <christia...@gmail.com> wrote:

Thanks for jumping in and helping answer questions!  A bit more below.

> Hi Stéphane,
>
> The warning is quite explicit: the matrix failed the positive definite test by a really really small number. This is a pretty common problem with priors on multivariate distribution.
>
> A good exercise in frustration with this problem is to try to sample from a multivariate distribution with the package MASS in R with what you believe to be a positive-definite symmetric covariance matrix. Most often than not the matrix is not exactly positive-definite and you will have to thinker with it with and use a function like make.positive.definite() from the package corpcor to coerce the function to work.
>
> As stated in the message itself this is not a serious problem unless you see the message really frequently. The message will invariably appear a few time right after you initialized the model, it will probably pop up randomly during the adaptation phase. It should have disappeared completely by the time you reach the sampling stage.
>
> As far as your second question is concerned all models will be slower in stan compared to jags. I believe this is even more apparent for multivariate models. I'm pretty sure the manual had a section on this part at some point although I haven't read the newer versions.

I just want to clarify this one.  It's not always the case that
Stan will be slower per iteration.  There are some calculations where
doing all the conditionals winds up being very expensive.

> However, and this is really important, for simple models stan will converge more quickly and will produce a higher number of effective sample sizes. As far as my experience with more complex models the advantage of stan over jags is that the model will ultimately converge... something I never achieved with jags.
>

That was what motivated Andrew to hire us to build Stan in the first place :-)

And the ability to do some models that you can't express in JAGS.  You'll
find JAGS and BUGS only let you do conjugate models for multivariate models.
In those cases, they're definitely faster if you code a direct translation into
Stan.

Sometimes you can exploit the conjugacy in Stan directly (there's a simple

messages.subject: Approximating integer-valued latent variable
messages.subject_clean: Approximating integer-valued latent variable
messages.body_plain:
Hi Folks -

I'm hoping to use Stan to estimate a model in which I would historically have included an integer-valued latent variable, and was wondering if the approach I'm hoping to use would break the gradient for HMC sufficiently to make it more worthwhile to use a sampler that explicitly deals with integer-valued latent variables.

So, I have a dataset on pediatric hospital admissions from 3 large hospitals and am trying to estimate age-specific rates of diarrheal disease risk for children < 5 years old as a function of social and environmental covariates. I'm hoping to model the counts for each age/week using a Poisson log-linear model.

Unfortunately, one of the hospitals in my dataset only reported the year of birth for each child rather than their exact birthday or age at the date of admission. This means that each child has two possible ages, a_0 < a_1. We can model p(a_1 | year_birth, date_admission) as a bernoulli random variable, with success probability equal to the proportion of a full year elapsed between the date of admission in the year of birth and the end of the year.

If I were hand-coding this, I would use a Gibbs step to marginalize out the latent vars and get on with life, but I'm hoping to take advantage of the HMC in stan to efficiently incorporate some spatial random effects. Marginalizing these using the approach described in the Stan manual, i.e explicitly writing the mixture probabilities, isn't really feasible because there are many individuals with partially observed birthdays (~ 20K), making calculation of the possible counts and mixture weights prohibitively expensive.

An alternative approach would be to treat the birthday as a uniformly distributed RV on the range from [Jan1, Dec31] in the year of birth, and then to count the individual as a_0 if the estimated date of birth occurs after the date of admission in the birth year and a_1 otherwise.

This is of course not strictly kosher as far as Stan's sampler is concerned, but I was wondering if anyone had insight about whether this would interfere with the accurate estimation of the model and whether I would still get the benefits of HMC for the other truly continuous parameters. Any ideas/suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks!

-Jon Zelner

messages.body_plain:
To be pedantic, it's an attempt at a flat prior and is at once not a great approximation (mathematically)
and too good of an approximation (practically).

The problem is that priors like this place a tremendous amount of probability mass at events way out
in the tails.  With little data your chains would spend most of their time around 1000, and if you seed
everything at O(1) the sampler will take forever to get out that far.  When you do have data but
your posterior is nasty and nonlinear the prior won't do anything, and you won't get any helpful
regularization.

But you have to deal with that, because if you set your prior to N(0, 1000) you're saying that 1000 is a
perfectly reasonable value (that's what Bob meant when he said "expect Mu to be huge").  If you consider
values that large to be extreme then your prior shouldn't be N(0, 1000).  If 1000 isn't that extreme then
you probably want to rescale your system so that expected values are O(1).

messages.body_plain:
There are two issues.

Firstly there's the computational issue of floating point arithmetic.  Manipulating numbers all of the same order
is much more stable and accurate then numbers of wildly varying scales.  The adaptation algorithm also
assumes that the typical set is near parameter values around 1, and if the typical set is actually way off at 1000
then it will take forever to reach and the chains will converge only slowly.

Then there's the modeling issue.  Flat priors are counter-intuitive (flat is not non-informative in R^n) and allow
likelihood pathologies (heavy-tails, extreme nonlinearities, etc) to propagate to the posterior.  Proper modeling requires
identifying the relevant scales and encoding them in our prior.

So if mu = 1000 is meaningful then go ahead and use it (although you really should rescale your problem to avoid
the computation issues noted above).  But it's just some arbitrary "big number" you should spend some more time
modeling your problem.

Categorical has two inputs, an integer and a vector of probabilities, and one output, a real-valued log probability density.
Your model defines k as a vector of reals, not integers, hence you're trying to insert a real into the integer argument which is causing the conflict.

That's why I don't know why there is a difference between 1000 * mu, mu ~ N(0, 1)  and  mu ~ N(0, 1000).  Where does this difference occurs in the algorithm ?

Stan samples from a given posterior, but an ill-conditioned posterior will lead to inefficient sampling.  For example, a model with many varying scales,

x1 ~ normal(0, 1);
x2 ~ normal(0, 1000);

will be difficult to sample from.  This often happens implicitly in complicated likelihoods, but restricting the prior to reasonable values prevents
an ill-conditioned likelihood from producing an ill-conditioned posterior; i's the same principle as regularization.  If you are not familiar with
these ideas I recommend you check out any decent book on MCMC -- http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/book/ and http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/arm/
provide thorough discussions.

messages.body_plain:
The third edition of BDA covers HMC and the principles are ARM are extremely relevant when one understands the possible pathologies of HMC.

Now floating point arithmetic has a limited bandwidth.  In one dimension N(0, 1000) sacrifices dynamic range for resolution where as 1000 * N(0, 1) provides better dynamic range at lower resolution.  In practice the resolution is
negligible compared to Monte Carlo errors and posterior variance, so 1000 * N(0, 1) is preferable, especially when your posterior is diffuse.  Additionally, 1000 * N(0, 1), makes it easier to define good default starting points
and integrator step sizes when initializing the algorithms.

What's most important, however, is the multivariate case where you have N(0, 1000) and N(0, 1).  Transforming to 1000 * N(0, 1) and N(0, 1) ensures that both parameters are O(1), there is approximate rotation invariance and
consequently the numerical integrator becomes significantly more accurate.  More accuracy means higher performance.

But these are all very specific to HMC or our implementation of it.  The bigger deal is that N(0, 1000) is a diffuse prior and diffuse priors are annoying to sample from (the extreme being an unbounded uniform distribution which
will never converge in more than 2 dimensions).  When your likelihood is not particularly informative the posterior defaults to this diffusive behavior, which is why we are careful to recommend relatively informative priors for
robust inference

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Understanding bad performance
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Understanding bad performance
messages.body_plain:
This is just a manifestation of concentration of measure — as the number of dimensions
increases the probability mass on a hypercube concentrates at the corners, and this
tends to overwhelm the posterior unless there is a tremendous amount of data.

Provided that you’re declaring your parameters as constrained between 0 and 1 then
there’s nothing inherently bad about approaching the boundaries.  On the unconstrained
scale the is exponentially more “room” near the boundaries so sampling should be okay,
if a bit slower.

What exactly is the N_eff / N ratio?  Does your model have hierarchical structure?  Is there
prior information you can impose to help constrain the values?  Honestly its just sounds like
you have a really, really big model with not a lot of information from the data/priors.

On Feb 26, 2014, at 6:54 PM, Kevin Van Horn <ke...@ksvanhorn.com> wrote:

> I  have a model that I'm having performance problems with -- a single update takes over 10 seconds, N_Eff is much less than 1/10 of the posterior sample size, and the tree depth after warmup averages 8 or 9. This model has over 8000 variables restricted to lie between 0 and 1. I thought that maybe the problem is due to variable values near the constraint boundaries. No single one of the variables has a mean closer than about 0.085 to one of the boundaries. However, with over 8000 variables, there tends to be at least one variable that is very close to a constraint boundary on any given time step. If I take the minimum (over all 8000+ variables) of the distance to a constraint boundary at every time step, the mean of this minimum over all time steps is about 6e-5.
>
> My impression is that even a single variable very close to a constraint boundary can cause problems. Is this correct? This suggests that my problem is simply that I have 8000+ interval-constrained variables that can plausibly vary over the entire interval; that is, I'm going to run into performance problems with ANY model that has such a large number of interval-constrained variables whose values can plausibly range over the entire interval. Is my thinking here correct?
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Results comparison of Stan and Winbugs
messages.body_plain:
Just taking a quick look, it doesn't look like the models are specified in the same way.

As an example, the prior for testlet is
WinBUGS:

> testlet1[j] ~ dnorm(0,tau1)
> testlet2[j] ~ dnorm(0,tau2)
> testlet3[j] ~ dnorm(0,tau3)
> testlet4[j] ~ dnorm(0,tau4)
> testlet5[j] ~ dnorm(0,tau5)
> testlet6[j] ~ dnorm(0,tau6)

where tau1 to tau6 are parameters (as far as I can tell)

Stan:

> testlet1 ~ normal(0,1);
> testlet2 ~ normal(0,1);
> testlet3 ~ normal(0,1);
> testlet4 ~ normal(0,1);
> testlet5 ~ normal(0,1);
> testlet6 ~ normal(0,1);

It's great that you're trying to do the comparisons. Just a couple notes:
- it's easy, but tedious translating models from BUGS to Stan. A bunch of the developers have gone through the painstaking exercise of specifying models in the Stan language, so it can be done. You have to be very, very careful and understand the differences in parameterizations.
- make sure the data is being read in correctly. If I'm remembering correctly, I think BUGS reads in matrices in row-major order. Stan reads matrices in column-major order.

My suggestion is to try specifying the Stan model again because it isn't a translation of the WinBUGS model. It's a different model and it might be operating on "different" data. For more guidance, look through the BUGS models we've already translated.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow sampling and "WW is not positive definite" in wishart_log
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Slow sampling and "WW is not positive definite" in wishart_log
messages.body_plain:
Consider a three-dimensional model with parameters x, y, z.
Let the priors for each be N(0, 1000) but the likelihood only constrains y, z with N(0, 1).
Then the posterior is still N(0, 1000) in the x direction.

The point is that the likelihood is often uninformative on some subset of the parameters
(or, even worse, some nonlinear combination of the parameters).  Good choices of prior
distributions consistent with actual prior expectations helps to regularize such likelihoods.

Hello,

I am fitting a model to data sets which have been simulated to display properties of a 2x2 design, each factor having two levels. There are two fully crossed groups, representing “subjects” and “items”. I constrain the groups' random intercepts and slopes to display certain patterns of correlation, which I give below. The known population parameters for correlation are denoted rho_subj and rho_item and the known sample correlations are denoted r_subj and r_item. The function two_by_two_gen.R which generated this data set is attached.

              intercept-factorA    intercept-factorB    factorA-factorB

rho_subj  0.6                       0.6                       0.6

r_subj      0.505                   0.629                    0.507

rho_item  0                         0                          0

r_item     0.147                   0.115                    -0.050

I let the eta parameter of the lkj correlation matrices vary among the values 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, and 4. For any given fit the lkj prior for the by-subject and the by-item correlation matrices have the same eta-parameter. The RStan code is given in the file two_by_two_sens_sim.R. Note that there are five models, and they differ only with respect to the shape parameter eta.

In general, the results are consistent with my expectations. More posterior density lies over the interval [0,1] than over the interval [-1,0]. This should obviously be the case for by-subject random effect correlations, since the known correlation parameters are positive. For by-item random effect correlations, however, the population correlation parameters are zero. For lower eta, we know that the estimates are going to be less conservative, and indeed they are. But it is worrisome to me that they always choose to go rightward, even for the correlation between slopes, whose sample correlation is somewhat negative. I had R write a PDF file with the plotted posterior pdfs for the by-item rhos.

I worry that this has to do with the direction of the fixed effects, which are both positive. But the fixed effects should be independent of the random effects, and of course also independent of the correlations between these. Has anyone experienced this before? Thanks for your help.

messages.body_plain:
I'd like to emphasise Michael's point that if the variables are constrained in the definition, then in a sense the boundaries are not boundaries at all. (Is it even possible to set up priors that make the sampler diverging on the unconstrained scale?)

In general, it is not always easy to find out why sampling is slow. Seemingly minor details in priors or in the model may make a big difference. Sometimes adding parameters to the model to make it fit the data better makes sampling faster.

A good approach is to start with a small subset of data, if possible, to try out different parameterisations and priors.

(I have a model fit currently in rstan that has over 32,000 parameters, with about 300,000 samples. I managed to generate 100 samples in 6 hours, and n_eff is good enough for my purposes.)

On Wednesday, February 26, 2014 9:26:35 PM UTC+2, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> This is just a manifestation of concentration of measure — as the number of dimensions
> increases the probability mass on a hypercube concentrates at the corners, and this
> tends to overwhelm the posterior unless there is a tremendous amount of data.
>
> Provided that you’re declaring your parameters as constrained between 0 and 1 then
> there’s nothing inherently bad about approaching the boundaries.  On the unconstrained
> scale the is exponentially more “room” near the boundaries so sampling should be okay,
> if a bit slower.
>
> What exactly is the N_eff / N ratio?  Does your model have hierarchical structure?  Is there
> prior information you can impose to help constrain the values?  Honestly its just sounds like
> you have a really, really big model with not a lot of information from the data/priors.
>
> On Feb 26, 2014, at 6:54 PM, Kevin Van Horn <ke...@ksvanhorn.com> wrote:
>
> > I  have a model that I'm having performance problems with -- a single update takes over 10 seconds, N_Eff is much less than 1/10 of the posterior sample size, and the tree depth after warmup averages 8 or 9. This model has over 8000 variables restricted to lie between 0 and 1. I thought that maybe the problem is due to variable values near the constraint boundaries. No single one of the variables has a mean closer than about 0.085 to one of the boundaries. However, with over 8000 variables, there tends to be at least one variable that is very close to a constraint boundary on any given time step. If I take the minimum (over all 8000+ variables) of the distance to a constraint boundary at every time step, the mean of this minimum over all time steps is about 6e-5.
> >
> > My impression is that even a single variable very close to a constraint boundary can cause problems. Is this correct? This suggests that my problem is simply that I have 8000+ interval-constrained variables that can plausibly vary over the entire interval; that is, I'm going to run into performance problems with ANY model that has such a large number of interval-constrained variables whose values can plausibly range over the entire interval. Is my thinking here correct?

On Thursday, February 27, 2014 1:49:55 PM UTC+2, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>
> > (I have a model fit currently in rstan that has over 32,000 parameters, with about 300,000 samples. I managed to generate 100 samples in 6 hours, and n_eff is good enough for my purposes.)
>
> Wow, that's incredible!  Can you share some details of the model?  We're always looking for more success stories as they tend to be under-reported around these parts.  :-)

I could share the whole model, but it's not too entertaining, just a large sparse logistic linear "mixture model" with hierarchy, normal priors for parameters, etc. The model could be fitted with lme4, but initial tests did not look promising (convergence problems, I did not test lme4 thoroughly), so ended up using Stan. This is a toy project, so far at least. I estimated the abundance changes of Finnish butterflies from open data and tried to compensate for variation in observational intensity: https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/8403120/rhop.png. Most of the parameters are about abundance at locations, per species. Maybe they could be marginalised away.

As expected and already known, there is a southern invasion going on. If I manage to write a blog entry of the results, I'll share it here.

More professionally, I work in a "data scientist" consultant team, and we have played with Stan a lot and even used it in a couple of projects. Our problems often seem to be at the edge of scalability of current Stan and HMC, so we're impatiently waiting for posterior approximation techniques. :) That is, the problems are not really "big data" projects, but often too big to be conveniently estimated with Stan/HMC.  Still there is often enough structure making straightforward use of standard tools impossible or suboptimal. Stan and probabilistic programming in general have a huge potential in this niche, IMO.

Hi Jorge,

I'm still confused about the use of the variable k. It looks like in both the BUGS and Stan specification, it doesn't look like it ties into the model. What I'm looking at is, in Stan:

for (n in 1:N)

  k[n] ~ categorical(pcatTable[n]);

with both k and pcatTable being declared in the data block. The use of k[n] is deterministic and since both k and pcatTable are data, this "sampling" statement is essentially ignored in the model.

Questions:
In the BUGS model, are k and pcatTable also data?
In the Stan model, in the sampling statement
Y[n] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(beta[1]+beta[2]*env1[n]))
you only have beta[1] and beta[2], but in the BUGS model, you have

z[i] <- betas[1]+betas[2]*env1[i]+betas[3]*env2[i]+betas[4]*env1sq[i]

What happened to the rest of the betas?

> Finally, this is not a simple logistic regression. Is a logistic regression with measurement error, for which I have a discrete empirical distribution of covariate values for each observations.

Sorry -- wasn't implying that it was. I was just suggesting that you start with that model as an example.

I couldn't follow your second statement. Could you write it out in math? Maybe that'll help me understand. I'll try to outline my confusion:
"measurement": I am assuming your env1Table are your measurement data.
"logistic regression with measurement error": I don't see a noise model on the env1Table (in both BUGS and JAGS).
"I have a discrete empirical distribution": I understand that to mean that you have a probability mass function, specified as a matrix, that you pass into the Stan / BUGS model. Is that pcatTable (it's the only one with the right dimensions)? How are you modeling your measurement error with this data?

Sorry if these are really simple questions -- I feel like that last statement explains a lot of what you're thinking, but I just couldn't parse it.

On to the updated model:

data {
  int<lower=0> N; // number of sites

  int<lower=0> M; // number of possible values for all sites

  int<lower=0> O; // number of betas
  matrix[N,M] env1Table; //predictor env1 matrix

  int<lower=0,upper=1> Y[N];// outcome vector

  int k[N];//observed ks
}

transformed data {
  vector[N] env1;

  for (n in 1:N)

    env1[n] <- env1Table[n,k[n]];
}

parameters {
  real beta[O];
}
model {
  beta ~ normal(0,10);
  for (n in 1:N) {
    Y[n] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(beta[1]+beta[2]*env1[n]));
  }
}

At this point, I'm not sure what I did relative to your original model, but this one compiles. I think there were some scoping issues (dangling braces), which I assumed were just typos in copying the original model to the users list.

Daniel

messages.subject: cut revisited
messages.subject_clean: cut revisited
messages.body_plain:
Dear Andrew et al,

I beg your indulgence for posting a topic that is not strictly a Stan issue. I am posting it here because it follows up on an earlier thread (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-users/ruxPAhBPI4A/Aj-BvWGOlEQJ). In addition I am considering the use of an approach to "cut" in an analysis using Stan.

During the previous thread Andrew Gelman stated: "The reason why I (and others) perceive "cut" as bad news is because when you do "cut," you are no longer doing Bayesian inference.  To put it another way, if it's really true that you don't want inference going from A to B, I don't think you want it going from B to A either. Joint distributions go both ways."

I accept that this is true for formal fully Bayesian inference, but I also think that prevention of "Bayesian feedback" is a useful heuristic in some practical contexts. David Lunn et al (Pharmacokinet Pharmacodyn (2009) 36:19–38) attempt to make that case for PKPD modeling. In that context there are usually 2 categories of dependent variable data: PK and PD, typically plasma drug concentrations and one or more measures of drug effects. In a typical PKPD model the PD outcomes are assumed to be a consequence of the PK (among other covariates).

My rationale for using cut in PKPD modeling is the same (I think) as that expressed in Lunn et al. Bayesian PKPD modeling is an excellent formalism for dealing with uncertainty in the model parameters. However our inferences are also conditioned on the mathematical structure of our model. There is also uncertainty in the form of our model and we usually do not account for that in any formal way. In PKPD modeling there are usually 2 (or more) linked models: one for PK outcomes and one for PD outcomes where it is usually assumed that the PD outcomes are affected by the PK (but not the reverse though there are exceptions). In many cases the uncertainty in the PD submodel structure is substantially greater than that for the PK model structure. This is due in part to differences in our state of knowledge about the underlying processes that cause the observed magnitudes in PK and PD outcomes. In addition there is often interest in making inferences about both PK and PD. Given such intentions, the disparity in model uncertainty and the assumed causal path, I argue it is undesirable for the larger potential PD model misspecification to impact inferences regarding PK.

I am interested in hearing other viewpoints on questions like:
Do you agree that the disparity in submodel uncertainty is an issue to be addressed in some way in the data analysis?
Is the notion of "cutting feedback" from the PD data to the PK model a reasonable heuristic approach for addressing that issue, and, if not, what are the alternatives?
Couldn't "cut" in the PKPD application be interpreted as a Bayesian analysis in which the PK model predictions are considered covariate data rather than a component of the prior? This is an attempt to argue for treating "cut" as multiple imputation of data.
So the bottom line is that I am trying to make the case for "cut", or to provoke someone into setting me straight.

I should also mention that I am aware of Martyn Plummer's convincing criticism of the approach to "cut" used in BUGS (http://www.pages.drexel.edu/~mwl25/mcmski/slides/mp_cuts.pdf), so I am not arguing for that approach. Instead I plan to apply the multiple imputation approach he suggests.

Thanks,
Bill

>
> I would like to run Stan in parallel with the following code, which utilizes the mclappy function from the parallel package:
>   stan.par <- mclapply(1:n.chain, mc.cores=n.chain, FUN=function(chain) {
>       stan(model_code=stan.code, data=stan.data, iter=n.iter, chains=1,
>              warmup=n.warm, thin=n.thin, verbose=FALSE, chain_id=chain,
>              refresh=max(floor(n.iter/100), 1), pars=pars.to.save, seed=chain
>              )})
>
> This has worked well except when I try to run it on RStudio, which appears to suppress the progress bar updates from the respective chains. This is unfortunately because I am running some very long jobs and would like some sense of when they will finish. Changing to verbose=TRUE doesn't help things. I imagine that this problem is not unique to Stan, so has anyone encountered it before? If so, did you find a solution? Thanks for the help!
>
> Devin
